item.title: EU Funding and Tenders Portal Helpdesk: Ticket in 5 Steps
item.dc:creator: Aoba Works
item.description: How to use the EU Funding and Tenders Portal helpdesk: open an IT ticket in 5 steps, what to include, response times, and when to call your NCP instead.
item.content:encoded:
How this guide was made: drafted with AI assistance from the official sources linked below, then passed an automated editorial check before publishing. Our process

The EU Funding and Tenders Portal helpdesk is the IT Helpdesk. You contact it through an online contact form, which you find under Guidance & documents > Helpdesk & support > IT Helpdesk. You can also reach it from your user icon once you are logged in. It handles technical problems with portal tools such as submission, registration and EU Login. Questions about eligibility or what to write in a proposal go to a different service: the Research Enquiry Service, or your National Contact Point (NCP) for Horizon Europe (Online Manual – Help). If a submission fails because of a fault on the portal's side, you have 4 calendar days after the call closes to file a complaint through the same form (Complaints about failed submission).

Which option is right for you?

The right helpdesk depends on whether your problem is technical, legal/administrative or about content. This table matches common situations to the service to contact first.

Your situationWhat to pick firstFirst page to open
Beginner who can't log in, can't find the "Submit" button, or sees an error messageIT Helpdesk ticketIT Helpdesk contact form
Your organisation has no PIC yet and you have a legal question about validation or appointing a LEARParticipant Validation HelpdeskValidation form
Your organisation already has a PIC and validation has asked for documentsMessages tab in Manage my OrganisationsRegister an organisation (IT How To)
Daily work: a grant consultant or research office asking a Horizon Europe legal/financial questionResearch Enquiry ServiceR&I Contact us
Tight budget, first proposal, you need help on eligibility or fit in your own languageNational Contact Point (free)NCP directory
A question about one specific call (not Horizon Europe)The functional mailbox named in the call documentsCall topic page, "Topic conditions and documents"
A general question about the EUEurope DirectOnline Manual – Help

Here is the reason behind each pick. IT staff can see system logs but won't judge whether you are eligible. NCPs give free advice in your own language but cannot fix the portal. Validation staff deal with your organisation's legal data, not with your proposal.

What is the EU Funding and Tenders Portal Helpdesk?

The EU Funding and Tenders Portal Helpdesk is the IT Helpdesk "for IT-related questions" about the portal's tools and processes. The Online Manual lists it next to separate services for validation, Horizon Europe enquiries and general EU questions (Online Manual – Help).

The portal's Help page lists four routes:

  • IT Helpdesk: for IT-related questions, reached through the contact form.
  • Participant Validation Helpdesk: "for legal questions relating to participant validation and LEAR appointment if you have NOT registered an organisation yet". Organisations that are already registered use the messaging feature in Manage my Organisations instead.
  • Research Enquiry Service or your National Contact Point: for Horizon Europe questions.
  • Europe Direct: for general questions about the EU. Programme-specific questions go to the functional mailbox given in the call documents.

(All four routes are from the Online Manual – Help, as of October 2026.)

The IT Helpdesk staff work Monday to Friday during Central European Time working hours (SEP user manual mirror). Plan around that. If you open a ticket on Friday evening for a Monday deadline, nobody will read it on Saturday or Sunday.

Pitfall: people treat "helpdesk" as a single inbox. If you ask the IT Helpdesk whether your startup counts as an SME, or whether a cost is eligible, you will usually be sent somewhere else, and that costs you days. Work out which kind of question you have before you write. For sorting out the SME question itself, see EU Funding for SMEs: 7 Open 2026 Calls and How to Qualify.

How to submit a ticket to the EU Funding and Tenders Portal Helpdesk

Log in to the portal, open Guidance & documents > Helpdesk & support, click IT Helpdesk, choose the right domain, describe the problem and send it. The five steps below follow the labels used in the official IT How To pages.

  1. Log in with EU Login. Sign in at the Funding & Tenders Portal. If two-step verification is what's blocking you, try the fixes in EU Funding and Tenders Portal Two Factor Authentication 2026 before you write a ticket.
  2. Open the helpdesk page. From the top menu choose Guidance & documents, then Helpdesk & support, then click the IT Helpdesk icon. The Register an organisation guide describes exactly this path. If you are already logged in, the SEP manual also documents a shortcut: User icon > IT Helpdesk at the top right (SEP user manual mirror).
  3. Select the domain. For problems with the proposal submission system, the official instruction is to select the domain Submission of proposals (Submit a proposal – IT How To). Pick whichever domain matches where the error happened (registration, grant management and so on). A wrong domain can delay routing.
  4. Describe the problem and attach evidence. Enter "the details of the problem" in the form (Register an organisation) and attach a screenshot if you need to (SEP user manual mirror). The next section lists what to include.
  5. Submit and keep the reference. Send the form and save the acknowledgement or ticket number. Quote it in every follow-up message, and in any later complaint about a failed submission.

Example (illustrative): a university research office sees an error when it clicks Submit on a Horizon Europe proposal. It selects Submission of proposals, pastes the exact error text, attaches a screenshot showing the system clock, and gives the proposal ID and call identifier. That one message lets the helpdesk find the session in its logs without asking for anything more.

What information do you need to fill in the helpdesk ticket form?

You need the right domain, a precise description, the identifiers for your proposal or organisation, and a screenshot. The official pages confirm the domain selection, the free-text problem details and the screenshot attachment. The other items in the table are a checklist so the helpdesk doesn't have to write back to you.

ItemWhere it goesOfficially documented?Example value (illustrative)
DomainDomain drop-downYes, e.g. "Submission of proposals" (IT How To)Submission of proposals
Problem detailsFree-text descriptionYes (Register an organisation)"Clicking Submit returns 'Unexpected error' since 10:42 CET"
ScreenshotAttachmentYes, "if required" (SEP manual mirror)PNG of the error with the clock visible
Proposal ID / call identifierDescriptionRecommendedProposal 101xxxxxx, HORIZON-CL5-2026-...
PIC (9 digits)DescriptionRecommended999999999 (example)
EU Login e-mailDescription, if different from the account you are writing fromRecommendedname@university.eu
Browser, version, operating systemDescriptionRecommendedFirefox 131, Windows 11
Timestamp and time zoneDescriptionRecommended2026-10-24 10:42 CET
Deadline date and timeDescriptionRecommendedCloses 2026-10-28 17:00 Brussels time

Write the description in this order: what you were doing, what you expected, what happened instead, and what you have already tried. For example: "Uploading Part B (PDF) in step 5 of the submission wizard. Expected the upload to complete. Got 'File could not be uploaded' three times. Tried Chrome and Firefox and cleared the cache."

Pitfalls and fixes

  • Vague subject lines like "Urgent!!" or "Portal not working". Fix: put the deadline and the proposal ID in the first line of the description.
  • Screenshots that hide the URL bar or clock. Fix: capture the full window. If you later file a complaint, you'll need these screenshots as proof of the failure (Complaints about failed submission).
  • Sharing your password. Your EU Login username and password are personal, and the manual says not to share them with anyone (Online Manual – EU Login). Never put them in a ticket.

How long does the EU Funding and Tenders Portal Helpdesk take to respond?

The portal pages reviewed for this guide publish no general response-time commitment for ordinary IT tickets. The one written timing is for failed-submission complaints, which get an acknowledgement "the same or next working day" (Complaints about failed submission, as of October 2026).

What the official sources do say:

  • Hours: Monday to Friday, during working hours CET (SEP user manual mirror). Weekends and EU public holidays are not covered.
  • Complaints: an acknowledgement the same or next working day. EU services then check the application and access log files, and tell you the outcome "as soon as possible" (Complaints about failed submission).
  • Submission timing advice: submit "at least 48 hours before the deadline" so you avoid problems with system requirements, local configuration settings and system congestion (Electronic proposal submission).

Read those three facts together. The portal assumes you'll have about two working days to spare if something breaks. If you open a ticket 6 hours before the deadline, you are relying on someone picking it up the same afternoon.

Pitfall: treating a ticket as a deadline extension. Opening a ticket doesn't stop the clock. The Submit a proposal guide says no changes are allowed once the closure date is reached. Keep trying alternatives (another browser, another network, a colleague's machine with their own login if they have a role on the proposal) while you wait for a reply.

IT Helpdesk vs National Contact Point: which one to contact

Contact the IT Helpdesk when the portal itself fails. Contact your NCP when you need advice on eligibility, fit or proposal content. NCPs are national structures that give "guidance, practical information and assistance on all aspects of participating in Horizon Europe" (R&I Contact us).

QuestionIT HelpdeskNational Contact PointResearch Enquiry Service
"Submit button returns an error"YesNoNo
"EU Login / 2FA won't accept my code"Yes (after the EU Login help FAQ)NoNo
"Is my NGO eligible for this topic?"NoYesYes
"Does my idea fit this call and expected outcomes?"NoYes, informal feedbackLimited
"How are personnel costs calculated?"NoYesYes
LanguageEnglishUsually your national languageEU languages
CostFreeFreeFree
Who it is not forContent or strategy questionsFixing system bugs, writing your proposal for youUrgent same-day technical fixes

NCPs exist in EU Member States and in countries associated with Horizon Europe. You find yours by country and theme in the NCP directory. Some NCP information is visible without logging in, and the rest only after login (UFUK Avrupa portal guide). One limitation: NCPs only cover Horizon Europe (and related programmes in some countries). For calls under other programmes, such as Digital Europe or LIFE, check the call documents for the right contact.

The Research Enquiry Service is the Commission-level alternative. It covers questions "about research in Europe, Horizon 2020 or other research programmes and funding instruments" (R&I Contact us). National agencies such as Austria's FFG send legal and financial Horizon Europe questions there (FFG).

Example (illustrative): a Spanish startup preparing an EIC application can't tell whether its pitch deck upload failed or was never needed. The upload error goes to the IT Helpdesk. The question "is a pitch deck required at this stage?" goes to the NCP, and the call documents answer it too. Dates for that programme are in EIC Accelerator Deadlines: 2026 Cut-Off Dates and Steps.

When should you escalate a helpdesk ticket?

Escalate when the problem blocks submission, the deadline is close, and you have had no useful answer. If the call has already closed and the portal was at fault, escalate by filing a formal failed-submission complaint within 4 calendar days.

The documentation reviewed here describes no "urgent" button or priority flag. In practice, escalating means adding information to the same ticket and, after closure, switching to the formal complaint route:

  1. Reply on the same ticket. Don't open a duplicate. Quote the original reference and add new facts: a new error text, a second browser tested, how many hours are left before the deadline.
  2. Name the deadline in the first line. For example: "Call closes 2026-10-28 17:00 Brussels time. Submission blocked."
  3. Keep preparing. Save timestamped PDFs of Part B and the annexes. File attributes that show when each file was created and last modified are what the complaint procedure asks for (Complaints about failed submission).
  4. After closure, file a complaint through the IT Helpdesk within 4 calendar days, with screenshots and the timestamped files. If the complaint is upheld, the files you supplied become your proposal for evaluation. If you supplied no files, the last version recorded in the system is used.
  5. Ask the right people in parallel. If the block is really a validation issue (for example a PIC that can't be attached), use the Messages tab in your organisation's record. If it's a programme question, contact the call's functional mailbox. Both are listed in the Online Manual – Help.

Pitfalls

  • Escalating a problem on your side. Complaints are checked against IT logs to confirm "technical problems on the Portal side". A slow office network or a corrupted PDF won't count.
  • Missing the 4-day window. Calendar days include weekends. If a call closes on Thursday, the window ends on Monday.
  • Asking an NCP to escalate a bug. NCPs can advise you, but they don't run the submission system.

Common errors reported to the EU Portal Helpdesk and how to fix them

Most tickets involve EU Login and two-step verification, PIC or LEAR validation, upload or submission errors near the deadline, and confusion about proposal status. Several of these can be fixed before you write a ticket.

EU Login and two-step verification. Lost phones, codes that are rejected and locked accounts are the most common blockers. Start with the official EU Login help FAQ. Two-step verification can be requested when you start a proposal or open drafts (Submit a proposal – IT How To), so set it up days in advance. Our two-factor authentication guide covers the setup.

PIC and LEAR problems. If your organisation hasn't registered yet, legal questions about validation go to the Participant Validation Helpdesk form, not to IT. Once you have a PIC, talk to the validation team through the Messages tab of your Organisation Data Update screen (Register an organisation). If a form crashes during registration, that is an IT ticket. The full registration flow is in EU Funding and Tenders Portal Registration: PIC in 6 Steps.

Upload and submission errors. The manual names three causes: system requirements, local configuration settings and system congestion. Before you open a ticket:

  • Try a second supported browser and switch off extensions.
  • Re-export the PDF. Flatten forms and remove encryption or passwords.
  • Check the page limits and file formats in the call's templates.
  • Submit early and resubmit if you need to. "Every submitted version will replace the previous one" (Electronic proposal submission).

Page-limit problems often surface only at the last validation step. Horizon Europe Proposal Template Part B: 2026 Scoring Map shows where the limits apply.

"Did it actually submit?" Many tickets are really status questions. Check the proposal's status in My Proposals before you write. Our My Proposals status table explains what each status means.

Pitfall: sending one ticket that mixes several problems, for example "my 2FA fails and also is my budget eligible?" Split it. Send the technical part to IT and the rest to the NCP or RES.

What to do if the portal is down near a submission deadline

Record the failure with screenshots and timestamps, open an IT Helpdesk ticket that states the deadline, keep retrying, and watch for an official extension. If the call closes before you get through, file a complaint within 4 calendar days.

  1. Capture evidence straight away. Take full-screen screenshots with the time visible and note the exact error text. The complaint procedure names screenshots as proof of the failure (Complaints about failed submission).
  2. Freeze your files. Save the final Part B and annexes as PDFs before the deadline and don't edit them afterwards. The created and modified timestamps are your evidence.
  3. Open the ticket under Submission of proposals, with the proposal ID, call identifier and deadline in the first line.
  4. Retry from a different setup. Use another browser, another network, or another team member who has a role on the proposal. You can resubmit as many times as you like before closure.
  5. Watch for official notices. Check the call's topic page and the programme's news channels. The Commission has extended deadlines after portal failures before. For example, in May 2021 the EIC Pathfinder Open deadline was moved to 25 May 2021 at 17:00 CET after submission problems (ChatEIC report). Don't count on an extension. It is an exception, not a rule.
  6. After closure, complain within 4 calendar days if the portal was at fault, attaching your evidence. You'll get an acknowledgement the same or next working day.

Pitfall: waiting for an outage notice before you act. Document and submit tickets as it happens, because evidence gathered afterwards is weaker. And because the manual recommends submitting at least 48 hours early, a last-hour outage is the case where a complaint has the best chance. A problem on your own side does not qualify.

Next steps

You can sort out most helpdesk issues yourself today with three actions, and free official advisers cover most of the rest.

Do this today (DIY):

  1. Bookmark the IT Helpdesk contact form. Save a ticket template in your notes containing your PIC, EU Login e-mail and the proposal ID and call identifier, so you can paste it in seconds.
  2. Find your NCP for your theme in the NCP directory and save their e-mail address now, before you have a question.
  3. Put a reminder in your calendar 48 hours before your call deadline as a "submit by" date, in line with the Online Manual advice.

If you'd rather not do it yourself:

  • National Contact Points: free (as of October 2026; check the official page). They suit first-time applicants who want advice on eligibility and fit in their own language. They are not for anyone who wants their proposal written, and they cannot fix portal bugs.
  • Research Enquiry Service: free (as of October 2026; check the official page). It suits consultants and research offices with precise legal or financial questions about Horizon Europe. It isn't built for urgent technical fixes on deadline day.
  • Private grant consultants: paid, and priced by quote. Fees vary widely by scope and many combine a fixed fee with a success fee, so ask for a written quote (prices change; check with each provider). They suit teams with no time or experience, or ones applying to competitive calls such as the EIC. They are not for applicants who only have a technical portal problem, which the free IT Helpdesk handles. A consultant also can't get you faster IT support than you could get yourself.

Related guides on this site:

  • EU Funding and Tenders Portal Registration: PIC in 6 Steps
  • EU Funding and Tenders Portal Two Factor Authentication 2026
  • EU Funding and Tenders Portal My Proposals: Status Table
  • Cascade Funding Open Calls: Portal Filters and 2026 Dates

FAQ

Is the EU Funding and Tenders Portal Helpdesk free to use?

Yes. The IT Helpdesk is a European Commission service reached through a free online form. NCPs and the Research Enquiry Service are free too. You only pay if you choose to hire a private consultant.

Can you contact the helpdesk by phone instead of a ticket?

The contact form is the documented main channel. A phone number (+32 2 29 92222) and the e-mail address EC-FUNDING-TENDER-SERVICE-DESK@ec.europa.eu appear in the Commission's SEP evaluation quick guide for technical SEP issues (SEP Expert Evaluation guide). Even if you call, open a written ticket as well, because complaints depend on a written record.

What is the difference between the IT Helpdesk and the Research Enquiry Service?

The IT Helpdesk handles IT-related questions about portal tools, such as submission errors, registration forms and login problems. The Research Enquiry Service answers questions about research programmes and funding instruments, including legal and financial points for Horizon Europe (R&I Contact us).

Do you need an EU Login account to submit a helpdesk ticket?

The documented route to the IT Helpdesk is through the portal, and the form is easiest to reach once you are logged in through the user icon. If EU Login itself is the problem, start with the EU Login help FAQ. The Guidance & documents > Helpdesk & support menu can be opened without logging in.

item.title: EIC Pathfinder 2026: Deadlines, 3 Challenges & 7 Steps
item.dc:creator: Aoba Works
item.description: EIC Pathfinder 2026 explained. Open closed 12 May, Challenges close 28 October 2026, with a €262M budget, 3 topics, page limits and steps to submit.
item.content:encoded:
How this guide was made: drafted with AI assistance from the official sources linked below, then passed an automated editorial check before publishing. Our process

The only EIC Pathfinder 2026 call you can still apply to is Pathfinder Challenges. It closes on 28 October 2026 at 17:00 Brussels time and has €96 million to share across three topics (EIC Pathfinder page, Euresearch). Pathfinder Open 2026 closed on 12 May 2026, and its 43 winners were announced on 14 October 2026 (EIC news). Neither 2026 Pathfinder call uses a "short proposal first, full proposal later" process. That two-step flow belongs to the EIC Accelerator, and it is only proposed for Pathfinder Open from 2027 (KoWi).

Which option is right for you?

Your best route depends on whether you already have a finished proposal on one of the three Challenge topics. Everyone else should get ready for the 2027 cycle.

Your situation (as of 23 October 2026)What to pick firstFirst page to open
Your proposal fits one of the three 2026 Challenge topics and is almost doneSubmit to Pathfinder Challenges before 28 Oct, 17:00 CETChallenges topic page on the Funding & Tenders Portal
You're a beginner with an early-stage (TRL 1–4) idea and no proposal yetSkip 2026. Prepare for the 2027 Pathfinder Open stage-1 short proposal (draft date 25 Feb 2027)EIC Pathfinder overview
You submitted to Pathfinder Open 2026 and weren't selectedRead your Evaluation Summary Report, then plan a 2027 resubmissionFunding & Tenders Portal → My Area → My Proposals
You're a company with a prototype (TRL 6–8) that's heading to marketEIC Accelerator, not PathfinderEIC Accelerator page
You're a consultant or grants office handling several clientsCheck each client's TRL and team shape against the table in the Open vs Challenges sectionEIC Work Programme 2026 (PDF)
You have a small budget and no consortiumPathfinder Challenges is the only Pathfinder strand that accepts a single applicantEuresearch Pathfinder summary

If you don't have a PIC (Participant Identification Code) yet, read EU Funding and Tenders Portal Registration: PIC in 6 Steps first. You can't submit without one.

EIC Pathfinder 2026 Call: What's Open Right Now?

Right now, only Pathfinder Challenges 2026 is open, until 28 October 2026. Pathfinder Open 2026 has closed and its results are out. Both run under the EIC Work Programme 2026 (Commission Decision C(2026) 4080). Each is a separate call with its own identifier, budget and deadline, and you can't move a proposal from one to the other.

Sub-callCall identifierOpenedDeadlineBudgetStatus (Oct 2026)
Pathfinder OpenHORIZON-EIC-2026-PATHFINDEROPEN-015 Feb 202612 May 2026, 17:00€166MClosed; 43 projects selected
Pathfinder ChallengesHORIZON-EIC-2026-PATHFINDERCHALLENGES-0122 Jul 202628 Oct 2026, 17:00€96MOpen

Sources: EIC Pathfinder page, Navarrabiomed call summary, euacc.ai DeepRAP call page, as of October 2026.

Some search results and older blog posts cause confusion:

  • One consultancy article gives 22 July 2026 as the Challenges deadline (Accelopment). That was the opening date. The EIC and national contact points give 28 October as the deadline.
  • Many pages list a run of 2026 dates: 7 January, 4 March, 6 May, 8 July, 2 September and 4 November. Those are EIC Accelerator full-proposal cut-offs (EIC Accelerator page), not Pathfinder dates. Pathfinder has one deadline per sub-call per year.
  • The EIC also runs Pathfinder Booster grants, a fixed amount of up to €50,000 for exploring commercialisation (EIC Pathfinder page). You can't apply for these directly. They're for teams that already hold a Pathfinder grant.

EIC Pathfinder Open vs Pathfinder Challenges: What's the Difference?

Pathfinder Open takes bottom-up ideas in any field. Pathfinder Challenges funds work only on topics the Commission defines in advance. The two also differ on team rules, page limits and how proposals are selected.

Pathfinder Open 2026Pathfinder Challenges 2026
TopicAny science-to-technology breakthrough3 fixed topics (see below)
Minimum team3 independent legal entities from 3 different Member States/Associated Countries, at least one in an EU Member StateSingle legal entity allowed (not mid-caps or large companies), or consortia of 2+
Part B page limit (sections 1–3)22 pages30 pages
Indicative grantUp to €4MUp to €4M (€500k–€4M range quoted)
SelectionRanked on scoresScores, then portfolio balancing by the Evaluation Committee
Extra obligation—A portfolio work package of at least 10 person-months
Funding modelLump sum, 100% of eligible costsLump sum, 100% of eligible costs

Sources: EU-Büro des BMFTR, EIC Pathfinder page, TPM Science, euacc.ai, as of October 2026.

Both strands are aimed at TRL 1–4, meaning early-stage work up to proof of concept (EIC Pathfinder page). Both also use the same award criteria and weights: Excellence 50% (threshold 4/5), Impact 30% (threshold 3.5/5), and Quality and efficiency of implementation 20% (threshold 3/5) (TPM Science). The Excellence threshold is high. A proposal that scores 3.5 there fails, however strong its impact section is. Our Horizon Europe Part B scoring map shows how to map each section to these criteria.

The portfolio step changes how Challenges proposals are written. After the remote scoring, the Evaluation Committee sorts proposals into categories and chooses "a balanced portfolio of diverse and complementary proposals" (TPM Science). For the DeepRAP topic, for example, the call text lists three dimensions: cognitive function (reasoning, abstraction, planning), technological approach (neuro-symbolic AI, deep learning, reinforcement learning and others) and use case (industry, health, cybersecurity and more) (euacc.ai). If your proposal is the fifth one on the same approach and use case, it can lose out to a lower-scoring proposal that fills a gap. State clearly which slot you fill.

Pick Open if you have three or more partners in different countries and an idea that doesn't fit a Challenge topic. Pick Challenges if your idea matches a topic, you are a single university lab or small firm, or you want the 30-page limit. Challenges suits you less if you dislike shared portfolio work, because the 10 person-months for portfolio activities come out of your project effort.

EIC Pathfinder 2026 Deadline: When Do I Need to Submit?

You need to submit to Pathfinder Challenges by 28 October 2026, 17:00 Brussels time. The Pathfinder Open 2026 deadline (12 May 2026) has passed. Each 2026 call had a single deadline for a full proposal. There were no short-proposal and full-proposal cut-offs (EU-Büro des BMFTR, euacc.ai).

If you're submitting to Challenges this week, use this sequence:

  1. Log in to the Funding & Tenders Portal with your EU Login. Set up two-factor authentication in advance if you haven't done so (our 2FA guide).
  2. Open the topic page for your challenge (HORIZON-EIC-2026-PATHFINDERCHALLENGES-01-01, -01-02 or -01-03).
  3. Scroll to the Submission service section and click Start submission. Enter the coordinator's PIC and a short title.
  4. Fill in Part A online: participants, contacts and the budget table. Follow the budget structure the submission form asks for, and check it against the Lump Sum Model Grant Agreement listed on the topic page.
  5. Upload Part B as a PDF. Sections 1–3 must not exceed 30 pages. Check the standard application form on the topic page for how over-length proposals are handled.
  6. Click Validate, fix any blocking errors, then click Submit.
  7. Check that the proposal status in My Proposals reads "Submitted" and that you received the confirmation email.

Common mistakes and fixes:

  • Submitting at 16:55. A last-minute upload leaves no time to fix validation errors or login problems. Submit a complete draft a day early, and check the Portal's guidance on replacing a submitted version before the deadline.
  • Wrong time zone. 17:00 Brussels is 16:00 in London and Lisbon, and 11:00 in New York at the end of October.
  • The coordinator's PIC isn't validated yet. Submission still works with a registered PIC, but tell the Validation Services early. Our PIC registration guide covers this.

How Does the EIC Pathfinder Open 2026 Deadline Work (Short vs Full Proposal)?

For Pathfinder Open 2026 there was no short proposal. Applicants submitted one full proposal by 12 May 2026, and the call received 2,103 proposals (Accelopment, Navarrabiomed). The short-then-full model is what changes in 2027, and it is still a draft.

According to the draft EIC Work Programme 2027 as reported in August 2026 (KoWi, evolution-europe, euacc.ai):

Stage (draft 2027)What you submitDraft dateEvaluated on
Stage 1Short proposal, max 8 pages, plus commitment letters from all partners25 February 2027Excellence and Impact only
Stage 2 (invited only)Full proposal, max 23 pages16 September 2027All three criteria
InterviewPitch of up to 10 minutes~10–14 weeks after stage 2—

The draft has no fixed score threshold at stage 1. The EIC ranks proposals and invites enough to stage 2 to cover about 2.5 times the available budget (KoWi). The draft budget stays at €166 million (Accelopment).

What this means for you:

  1. The 2027 clock starts in February, not May. That leaves about four months after the Work Programme is adopted (expected in early November 2026, per the EIC).
  2. Get partner commitment letters early. A consortium you put together in the last week won't meet a stage-1 requirement for signed letters.
  3. You can't skip stage 1. Only invited applicants can submit at stage 2. If you miss 25 February 2027, you would wait for the 2028 cycle.
  4. Don't plan around draft dates as if they were final. Both KoWi and the EIC say the details can change before adoption. Check the final Work Programme PDF once it's published.

What Are the EIC Pathfinder 2026 Challenges (Topics)?

The 2026 Pathfinder Challenges are three topics, each with about €32 million: miniaturised energy harvesting materials, biotechnology for healthy ageing, and trustworthy cognitive AI (TPM Science, Zabala).

Topic codeChallengeIndicative budgetEach topic has its own Challenge Guide?
HORIZON-EIC-2026-PATHFINDERCHALLENGES-01-01Advanced Materials for Miniaturised Energy Harvesting Systems€32MYes
HORIZON-EIC-2026-PATHFINDERCHALLENGES-01-02Biotechnology for Healthy Ageing€32MYes
HORIZON-EIC-2026-PATHFINDERCHALLENGES-01-03DeepRAP: Deep Reasoning, Abstraction & Planning towards trustworthy Cognitive AI Systems€32MYes

Sources: Microfluidics Innovation Center call list, euacc.ai, as of October 2026.

With a typical grant of €4 million, €32 million per topic works out to about eight projects. The DeepRAP call page gives the same figure (euacc.ai). Competition was tough in earlier years too. In 2025 the Challenges success rate was 4.5%, and demand was 19.2 times the available budget (Zabala).

Each topic has its own Challenge Guide, written by the EIC Programme Manager in charge. It sets out the specific objectives and the portfolio categories. Read it before you read the generic Work Programme text. A proposal that is excellent but doesn't connect to the Guide's objectives is likely to lose points on Excellence.

The 2027 Challenge topics will be different. The draft 2027 Work Programme contains three new draft Challenges (KoWi), so don't assume the 2026 topics will come back.

What Is the EIC Pathfinder 2026 Budget?

The EIC Pathfinder 2026 budget is €262 million: €166 million for Open and €96 million for Challenges. Grants are usually up to €4 million per project, and more is possible if it is "duly justified" (EIC Pathfinder page, Zabala).

ItemFigureSource (as of Oct 2026)
Total Pathfinder 2026€262MZabala
Pathfinder Open€166MEIC
Pathfinder Challenges€96M (€32M × 3)TPM Science
Grant per projectUp to €4M, more if justifiedEIC
Funding rate100% of eligible costs, lump sumTPM Science
Booster grant (grantees only)Fixed amount up to €50,000EIC
Pre-financing40–60%, within 30 days of signatureeuacc.ai

Because the grant is a lump sum, read the Lump Sum Model Grant Agreement on your topic page to see how payments are linked to the work you deliver. Your budget table still needs realistic costs per work package, since evaluators check whether the resources match the work. Asking for more than €4 million is allowed, but every extra euro has to be justified in the Quality and efficiency section, which carries only 20% of the score.

How to Find the EIC Pathfinder 2026 Template and Submission Documents?

The official templates are on each topic page of the Funding & Tenders Portal, under Topic conditions and documents. The general EIC website doesn't host the proposal forms (euacc.ai).

  1. Go to the Funding & Tenders Portal → Search funding & tenders → Calls for proposals.
  2. Type the call identifier, for example HORIZON-EIC-2026-PATHFINDERCHALLENGES-01, into the search box. Set the status filter to Open for submission.
  3. Click your topic (-01-01, -01-02 or -01-03).
  4. Open Topic conditions and documents and download:
  5. the EIC Work Programme 2026,
  6. the Challenge Guide for your topic,
  7. the standard application form (HE EIC Pathfinder Challenges), which is the Part B template,
  8. the standard evaluation form, which shows what evaluators score,
  9. the Lump Sum Model Grant Agreement.
  10. Check Topic updates on the same page for corrections or FAQ changes published after the call opened.
  11. To see the Word Part B template inside your draft, click Start submission and download it from the submission system. The version there is always the current one.

Common mistakes and fixes:

  • Using a 2024 or 2025 template. Page limits and sections change. Open used 22 pages in 2026, and the 2027 draft proposes 23 for stage 2 (euacc.ai). Download a fresh copy from this year's topic page.
  • Using the Open template for Challenges. They have different page limits (22 vs 30). The Challenges template also expects the portfolio work package.
  • Removing the template instructions but keeping the headings out of order. Evaluators score against the evaluation form headings, so keep the template's numbering.

EIC Pathfinder 2026 Timeline: From Submission to Grant Agreement

Expect results about 5 months after the deadline and a signed grant agreement about 8 months after it (TPM Science, euacc.ai). The 2026 Open call fits this pattern: deadline 12 May, results 14 October (EIC news).

For Pathfinder Challenges 2026, the EIC describes a two-step evaluation without an interview (TPM Science):

  1. Remote evaluation. At least three independent EIC expert evaluators score your proposal against the three criteria.
  2. Evaluation Committee. The committee, which includes EIC Programme Managers, builds the portfolio and may recommend small changes to strengthen links between projects.
  3. Information letter. Under the 5-month rule, this would come around late March 2027. This date is an example calculated from the rule, not an announced date.
  4. Grant agreement preparation. You finalise data, the budget and portfolio commitments in the Portal.
  5. Signature. Using the 8-month rule as an example, this would be around late June 2027. Pre-financing follows within about 30 days.

For a project you submit on 28 October 2026, this means work probably won't start before mid-2027. If you need bridge funding, apply for it separately. A Pathfinder grant won't fill a gap in early 2027.

EIC Pathfinder 2026 Results: Where to Check if You Were Selected?

Your own result comes to your EU Login account in the Funding & Tenders Portal, under My Area → My Proposals. The EIC publishes overall results, such as the 43 Pathfinder Open 2026 projects, on its news pages.

To check yours:

  1. Log in to the Portal and open My Area → My Proposals.
  2. Find your proposal and look at the status column. Our My Proposals status table guide explains each status.
  3. Open the evaluation result letter and the Evaluation Summary Report (ESR), which has the scores and comments for each criterion.
  4. If you were selected, watch for the grant agreement preparation invitation and the deadlines for responding.
  5. If you weren't, compare your scores against the thresholds (4 / 3.5 / 3). The ESR may also say if evaluators advise against resubmitting (euacc.ai).

Here are the published Pathfinder Open 2026 figures, so you can see where you stand. The EIC selected 43 projects involving 218 organisations from 30 countries. Of 266 participations, 44% were higher education institutions, 28% research organisations and 25% private companies, and 34 of the 43 projects include an SME (EIC news). From 2,103 submissions, that is a success rate of about 2% (Accelopment). A score just below the thresholds is common, and it doesn't mean the idea is bad.

EIC Pathfinder vs EIC Accelerator 2026: Which Call Should I Apply To?

Choose Pathfinder for research at TRL 1–4 that is heading toward a proof of concept. Choose the Accelerator if your company is at TRL 6–8 and is scaling toward the market. The two calls have different deadlines, templates and applicants (EIC Pathfinder, EIC Accelerator).

EIC Pathfinder 2026EIC Accelerator 2026
TRL1–46–8
Who appliesConsortia (Open), or single entities or consortia (Challenges)Single startups/SMEs (some others in specific cases)
MoneyGrant up to €4M, 100% lump sumGrant up to €2.5M plus €1M–€10M equity/quasi-equity
Process in 2026Single-stage full proposalShort proposal (12-page form, 10-slide deck, 3-min video) → full proposal → interview
2026 datesOpen 12 May; Challenges 28 OctShort proposals batched first Tuesday monthly; full cut-offs 7 Jan, 4 Mar, 6 May, 8 Jul, 2 Sep, 4 Nov

Sources: EIC official pages above, as of October 2026.

Pitfalls:

  • "Short proposal" searches often lead to Accelerator rules. If a page tells you to send a short proposal before a Pathfinder deadline, it either describes the Accelerator or the draft 2027 Pathfinder Open process.
  • The 4 November 2026 Accelerator cut-off is only open to companies whose short proposal already received a GO (EIC Accelerator). Our EIC Accelerator deadlines guide covers that timeline.
  • Applying too early for the Accelerator. If you have no prototype and no validation outside the lab, Pathfinder (or Transition, once you have Pathfinder results) is the better fit.

If neither fits your stage, our overview of EU funding for SMEs: 7 open 2026 calls lists other options.

Next steps

What you should do next depends on whether you're submitting this week or preparing for 2027.

Things you can do today:

  1. If you're submitting to Challenges, upload a complete draft today, validate it, and plan the final submission for 27 October, a day before the deadline.
  2. If you're preparing for 2027, write a one-page summary of your idea against the Excellence and Impact criteria only. Under the draft, stage 1 judges only those two. Then list the partners whose commitment letters you'll need by February.
  3. If you applied to Open 2026 and weren't selected, download your ESR from My Proposals and mark every comment below 4/5 on Excellence.

If you'd rather not do it yourself:

  • National Contact Points (NCPs) for the EIC are free, government-funded advisers in each Member State and Associated Country. Examples are the EU-Büro des BMFTR in Germany and Euresearch in Switzerland (as of October 2026; check the official page). NCPs are good for eligibility questions and proposal checks. They won't write the proposal for you, and they get very busy just before deadlines.
  • University research offices often review Pathfinder drafts for their own staff. Ask your office what support it offers and on what terms. This doesn't help startups without an academic partner.
  • Private grant consultancies will write or co-write proposals. Fees and fee structures vary a lot, so ask for a written quote. This option suits teams short on time and with a clear idea. It suits you less if the science still needs to be shaped by the researchers themselves. Evaluators score scientific vision most heavily, and nobody can outsource that.

FAQ

Is EIC Pathfinder Open 2026 still open?

No. Pathfinder Open 2026 closed on 12 May 2026, and 43 projects were announced on 14 October 2026. The next Pathfinder Open call is expected under the 2027 Work Programme, with a draft stage-1 deadline of 25 February 2027 that may still change.

What is in the EIC Pathfinder 2026 call?

It has two sub-calls: Pathfinder Open (€166M, any topic, closed) and Pathfinder Challenges (€96M, three topics, deadline 28 October 2026). Both fund TRL 1–4 research with lump-sum grants of up to €4 million per project.

What was the EIC Pathfinder Open 2026 deadline?

The deadline was 12 May 2026 at 17:00 Brussels time. It was a single-stage full proposal with a 22-page Part B, and 2,103 proposals were submitted.

What are the EIC Accelerator 2026 cut-off dates?

The 2026 full-proposal cut-offs are 7 January, 4 March, 6 May, 8 July, 2 September and 4 November. Short proposals can be submitted at any time and are batched on the first Tuesday of each month. Only applicants with a GO on their short proposal can use the 4 November cut-off.

item.title: EU Funding and Tenders Portal My Proposals: Status Table
item.dc:creator: Aoba Works
item.description: What each status in EU Funding and Tenders Portal My Proposals means, where to find your ESR and result letters, and what to do next, with menu paths.
item.content:encoded:
How this guide was made: drafted with AI assistance from the official sources linked below, then passed an automated editorial check before publishing. Our process

In the EU Funding & Tenders Portal, My Proposals (now listed as Proposals in the left-side menu) shows each application as a draft, submitted or withdrawn record. After the call closes, the outcome appears under three dots menu > Follow-up. Evaluation results, the Evaluation Summary Report (ESR) and your result letter are posted at My Proposals > three dots > Follow-up > Proposal Management & Grant Preparation > Documents (Online Manual). The status label tells you where the proposal is. The letter in that Documents folder tells you what to do next. This guide covers both.

Which option is right for you?

Pick your starting point from your current situation. You don't need to read every section if your status already tells you where you stand.

Your situationWhat to pick firstFirst page to open
First time using the portal, call still openCheck that the proposal says Submitted and download the time-stamped PDFProposals > three dots > View Submitted
You submitted but want to change something before the deadlineEdit and resubmit. The new version overwrites the old oneProposals > View Draft / Update
Call closed, waiting for resultsNote the "time to inform" date from the call, then leave it aloneTopic page of your call
Result letter arrived, not fundedRead the ESR, then decide on redress within 30 daysFollow-up > Proposal Management & Grant Preparation > Documents
Invited to grant preparationCheck roles, the LEAR and PIC validation, then start the grant dataMy Projects > three dots > Manage Project
Consultant or grant office handling many proposalsSwitch the filter from "last 180 days" to "All records"Proposals list filter
Tight budget, no consultantUse the free IT Helpdesk and your National Contact PointPortal Support page

A short reason for each choice: the time-stamped PDF is the only proof of what was received. Overwriting is allowed only until the deadline. The redress clock starts when you receive the letter, not when you happen to open it. The default 180-day filter hides older proposals, which catches out anyone tracking several calls (IT How To: Follow up your proposal).

If you can't log in or see the Proposals menu at all, sort out access first. Start with EU Funding and Tenders Portal Registration: PIC in 6 Steps and EU Funding and Tenders Portal Two Factor Authentication 2026.

Quick status decoder

The portal manual describes the lifecycle, but the wording on screen and in letters varies a little by programme. Use this table to translate each status.

What you seePlain meaningAction needed
DraftSaved but never sentSubmit before the deadline. Drafts stay readable for about 90 days after closure
SubmittedReceived. Only the latest version countsDownload and check the PDF. Otherwise wait
WithdrawnPulled from evaluationResubmit before the deadline if you want it evaluated
Under evaluation (after closure)Admissibility and eligibility checks, then expert scoringNone. Watch the date in the call
Rejected: inadmissible/ineligibleFailed formal checks, so it was not scoredRead the letter. Redress possible within 30 days
Rejected: below thresholdScored, but failed a thresholdRead the ESR. Redress only for procedural errors
Reserve listPassed thresholds, no budget yetWait. Keep the consortium available
Invited to grant preparationSelected, but not yet a legal commitmentStart grant preparation in Projects
FinalProcess closed, record kept for referenceArchive documents

Sources for the table: Follow up your proposal, Submit, Evaluation and evaluation results.

What does 'status: submitted' mean in My Proposals?

Submitted means the Commission received your proposal before the deadline. Only the most recent submitted version will be evaluated. After submission, the proposal has been "sent to the European Commission services for evaluation" (IT How To: Submit).

The status is not locked until the call closes, though. Until the deadline, the coordinator can keep editing and resubmitting, and "every submitted version will replace the previous one" (Online Manual: Electronic proposal submission). After the deadline, "no further corrections or re-submissions are possible", and you only have read-only access.

Steps to confirm a submission properly

  1. Log in and open Proposals in the left-side menu (older guides call it My Proposals).
  2. Find the proposal, click the three dots menu and choose View Submitted.
  3. Download the proposal. The portal provides "a digitally signed and time-stamped version of the latest submitted version" (Submit).
  4. Open the PDF and check that Part B is the right file, page counts fit the limit and all annexes are attached.
  5. Check the inbox of the coordinator's contact persons. "All contact persons of the coordinating organisation will receive an e-mail" with the e-receipt (Electronic proposal submission).

Pitfalls and fixes

  • The signed PDF isn't there yet. The time-stamped version "can take from a few seconds up to several hours to be visible" (Submit). Don't resubmit in a panic. Wait, then check again. This is one reason the portal advises submitting well ahead of the deadline.
  • A partner uploaded a newer Part B but nobody pressed Submit. Only the coordinator can submit (Proposal roles and access rights). An uploaded file sitting in a draft is not part of the submitted version.
  • Continuously open calls behave differently. "The re-edit functionality is not available for continuously open calls" (Electronic proposal submission), so check everything before you press Submit.

What does 'status: withdrawn' mean and can I resubmit?

Withdrawn means the coordinator removed the proposal from evaluation. You can undo it by resubmitting the same proposal before the call deadline. The portal says: "If your proposal is withdrawn, it will not be considered for evaluation. However, the system will keep the proposal draft and the withdraw action may be reversed by re-submitting the proposal before the call deadline" (Submit).

You don't create a new proposal. You resubmit the same record, which keeps its ID.

How to withdraw, and how to reverse it

  1. Go to My Proposals > View Submitted > Withdraw proposal (Step 6 of the submission wizard) (Electronic proposal submission).
  2. Type the reason for withdrawal. The field is required.
  3. Confirm. The Proposal Coordinator gets an email notification.
  4. To reverse it, open the draft again, make any changes and press Submit before the deadline. The status changes back to Submitted.

After the deadline, the self-service button is gone. "If you wish to withdraw a proposal after the deadline, you need to request it via the IT Helpdesk" (Submit).

Example

Here is an illustration. A consortium submits on Monday for a Thursday 17:00 Brussels-time deadline. On Tuesday, a partner says it can't sign up to the budget, so the coordinator withdraws the proposal. On Wednesday, a replacement partner is added in Step 4 and the coordinator presses Submit. Because this happens before the deadline, the proposal goes back to Submitted and will be evaluated. If the coordinator waits until Friday, the proposal stays withdrawn and is not evaluated.

Retention

Withdrawn proposals are accessible until the call closes and then "typically" for 90 days, although the "amount of days can differ from one call to another" (Follow up your proposal). Download your files before they disappear. The Delete Proposal action permanently removes drafts and withdrawn proposals, so only use it if you no longer need the content.

What does 'evaluation ongoing' mean and how long does it take?

After the deadline, your submitted proposal goes through admissibility and eligibility checks, then expert scoring. For most Horizon Europe calls, results arrive about 5 months after the deadline. The portal shows no step-by-step progress bar. Your proposal simply stays Submitted until a letter appears in Follow-up.

First, the granting authority checks admissibility ("complete and properly put together") and eligibility. Proposals that pass go to an independent evaluation committee (Admissibility and eligibility check). The evaluation itself has three steps: individual evaluation (usually "at least three individual evaluators"), a consensus group, and a panel review that ranks the proposals above the threshold (Evaluation and evaluation results).

Official timelines (Horizon Europe, as of October 2026)

Call typeResult ("time to inform")Grant signature ("time to grant")
Single-stage~5 months from deadline~8 months from deadline
Two-stage, stage 1~3 months from stage 1 deadline—
Two-stage, stage 2~5 months from stage 2 deadline~8 months from stage 2 deadline

Sources: Horizon Europe Work Programme General Annexes (2026-2027 General Annexes) and NCP Flanders two-stage infosheet. REA gives the evaluation phase as "up to five months" (REA: How to apply). The topic's call conditions always take priority over these defaults. The Online Manual says the timing for your call is in the call conditions on the Topic page (Evaluation and evaluation results).

Other programmes, such as Erasmus+, CERV, LIFE and Digital Europe, set their own dates. EIC Accelerator cut-offs also follow their own rhythm. See EIC Accelerator Deadlines: 2026 Cut-Off Dates and Steps. For a two-stage example with real dates, see HORIZON-HLTH-2027-02-TOOL-01-two-stage: Dates & Page Limits.

What to do while waiting

  1. Write the "time to inform" date from your topic page into the consortium calendar.
  2. Make sure the coordinator's contact persons keep valid accounts and 2FA. Results go "through the coordinating organisation".
  3. Don't contact evaluators or ask for interim scores. You won't get them.

What does 'above threshold but not retained' mean?

Your proposal passed every quality threshold but ranked below the budget cut-off. It is either on a reserve list or rejected because the money ran out. The portal manual says a proposal must score above each criterion threshold and the overall threshold, and also be "ranked sufficiently to be above the budget-threshold (relative positioning in the list of all proposals)" (Award criteria).

So there are two different bars. The quality threshold is absolute. The budget threshold is relative and depends on how many good proposals competed for the same topic budget.

Reserve list vs rejection

  • Reserve list. "If the available budget is too small to fund all above-threshold proposals, some proposals may be put on a reserve list. These will then be offered funding if a higher-scoring project does not go ahead or additional funds become available" (Evaluation and evaluation results).
  • Rejected despite being above threshold. If no reserve list is kept, or your rank is too low for it, you get a rejection letter even though your scores passed.

Example

Here is an illustration with made-up numbers. A topic has a budget for three projects. Your proposal scores 12.5/15, which clears the 10-point threshold. Five proposals scored 13 or higher, so yours ranks sixth. The letter puts you on the reserve list at position 3. You are funded only if three higher-ranked projects drop out or extra budget appears.

Pitfalls and fixes

  • Treating reserve as rejection. Partners may commit staff to other projects. Keep the consortium informed and available until the letter says the list is closed.
  • Filing redress because "the score was high enough". Redress covers procedure, not merits (see the FAQ). A good score that ranked too low is not a procedural error.
  • Resubmitting unchanged. The ESR comments show where you lost the half-points that cost you your rank. Fix those first. Our Part B scoring map links each criterion to the template sections.

How do I read the Evaluation Summary Report (ESR) scores?

In Horizon Europe, the ESR gives a score from 0 to 5 for Excellence, Impact and Implementation. The threshold is 3 per criterion and 10 out of 15 overall, unless the call says otherwise (General Annexes). Half-marks are allowed, according to the official evaluation forms (HE RIA/IA evaluation form).

Score meanings (Horizon Europe evaluation forms)

ScoreLabelWhat the experts mean
0—Fails to address the criterion, or can't be assessed because information is missing
1PoorInadequately addressed, or serious inherent weaknesses
2FairBroadly addressed, but significant weaknesses
3GoodAddressed well, but a number of shortcomings
4Very goodAddressed very well, with a small number of shortcomings
5ExcellentAll relevant aspects addressed; any shortcomings are minor

Source: Horizon Europe evaluation form (RIA/IA).

Thresholds by stage (as of October 2026)

StageCriteria scoredPer-criterion thresholdOverall threshold
Single-stage / stage 2Excellence, Impact, Implementation310 of 15
Two-stage, stage 1Excellence, Impact only4Set so that the stage-2 budget is close to 3× the available budget (not less than 2×)

Sources: General Annexes, NCP Flanders. Other programmes use other criteria, such as "relevance" in Erasmus+, and other thresholds. The Online Manual says the labels "vary" and refers you to the call conditions (Award criteria).

How to read the report

  1. Check each criterion score against the threshold first. One score of 2.5 rules out funding, whatever the total.
  2. Read the comments under each criterion. They are the consensus view, not one evaluator's opinion. During evaluation, each expert writes an individual evaluation report (IER), and the ESR merges them (Online Manual).
  3. Check that each comment matches its score. If the text lists only strengths but the score is 2, that mismatch is a legitimate redress ground ("lack of coherence between scores and comments") (Complaints about proposal rejection).
  4. Turn each listed shortcoming into a fix for your next submission.

A two-stage detail: successful stage-1 applicants get no ESR at that point. "The Commission publishes generalised feedback", and the stage-1 ESR arrives later together with the stage-2 result (NCP Flanders).

What does 'Grant Agreement Preparation (GAP) started' status mean?

It means you received a grant preparation invitation letter. The coordinator must now enter the grant data, and all partners must clear legal and financial validation. It does not yet mean you have the money. The manual is explicit: "invitation to grant preparation is NOT a formal commitment for funding" (Evaluation and evaluation results).

Selected proposals move from Proposals to Projects. To open them, click the three dots and choose Manage project, which takes you into the Grant Management Services system (Follow up your proposal).

Steps for the coordinator

  1. Open My Projects > three dots > Manage Project > Proposal Management & Grant Preparation > Grant agreement data preparation (Grant preparation).
  2. Check the roles. The minimum set is the coordinator's Primary Coordinator Contact (PCoCo), the LEAR and the Project Legal Signatory (PLSIGN). Each other beneficiary needs a Participant Contact (PaCo), a LEAR and a PLSIGN (Online Manual v1.1).
  3. Ask every partner without a validated PIC to answer the Central Validation Service quickly. Each organisation also has to appoint its LEAR.
  4. Have partners enter their own legal, administrative and financial data.
  5. Finish the Description of Action. Part A tables are filled in by the system. Part B is the narrative PDF based on your proposal. Make sure it matches any changes requested in the invitation letter.
  6. Complete the work plan tables, deliverables and milestones. Then submit the grant data, which triggers Final legal checks and Grant signature (Grant preparation).

At the same time, the granting authority runs legal entity validation, a financial capacity check and non-exclusion checks. If your topic involves ethics or security issues, those reviews also happen before signature. Ethics results are posted at My Projects > three dots > Manage Project > Document Library (Special procedures). Ethics requirements can become extra deliverables in a work package the system creates automatically.

Pitfall: an SME partner registered quickly, but its PIC was never validated, and that stalls the whole consortium. To avoid this, validate PICs as early as possible (PIC registration guide).

How to check who is assigned as coordinator vs partner in a proposal?

Open the proposal and look at Step 3 (coordinator) and Step 4 (participants) of the wizard. After the call closes, use Proposals > three dots > Manage Consortium. Submission roles are "managed in the proposal itself", not through the portal's general Manage Roles function (Proposal roles and access rights).

Steps

  1. Before the deadline, open the draft with Edit Draft. Step 3 shows the coordinating organisation and its PIC. Step 4 lists each participant with its contact persons (Electronic proposal submission).
  2. For each contact person, check the access type: full access, or read-only (Team Member).
  3. After the call closes, use Manage Consortium. Changes there affect only who can see the proposal, not who is in the consortium.

Roles at a glance

Proposal roleCan submit/withdraw?Becomes after funding
Proposal Coordinator (main contact)Yes, the only role that canPrimary Coordinator Contact (PCoCo)
Coordinator contact person, full accessEdits; submission is the coordinator'sCoordinator Contact (CoCo)
Coordinator contact person, read-onlyNoTeam Member (TeMe)
Partner main contactNoParticipant Contact (PaCo)
Affiliated entity / associated partnerNoAffiliated entities can't take administrative actions; associated partners can't claim costs

Source: Proposal roles and access rights. The person who starts the proposal becomes its main coordinator contact.

Example: a university research office creates the proposal for a professor, so the office's staff member becomes the main coordinator contact. If that person goes on leave, nobody else can submit unless a full-access contact was added in time. Add a second full-access contact for the coordinator early.

How to download the proposal and evaluation documents from My Proposals?

You get the submitted PDF from View Submitted. Result letters and the ESR are at Follow-up > Proposal Management & Grant Preparation > Documents. In the newer grants interface, they are filed under "Process documents" in the project document library (Redress).

Steps

  1. Open Proposals and set the filter to All records if the proposal is older than 180 days (Follow up your proposal).
  2. For the proposal itself, go to three dots > View Submitted and download the signed, time-stamped PDF.
  3. For results, go to three dots > Follow-up. Then open Proposal Management & Grant Preparation > Documents. You'll find the ESR and the rejection, reserve or invitation letter there (Evaluation and evaluation results).
  4. Inadmissible or ineligible proposals get their rejection letter in the same place: My Proposals > Actions > Follow-up > Proposal Management & Grant Preparation > Documents (Admissibility and eligibility check).
  5. For ethics review results on funded projects, go to My Projects > Manage Project > Document Library.

Save copies outside the portal. Unsuccessful proposals stay visible in "final" status for "3/5 years (varies from programme to programme)", and drafts and withdrawn records disappear after about 90 days (Follow up your proposal).

Next steps

Today, take one or more of these steps.

  1. Open Proposals, switch the filter to All records and download the time-stamped PDF of every submitted proposal you're responsible for.
  2. For any proposal with a result letter, write down the date you received it and the date 30 days later. That is your redress deadline (Redress).
  3. If you were invited to grant preparation, ask every partner to confirm that its PIC is validated and that a LEAR is appointed.

If you'd rather not do this yourself, you have two main options:

  • National Contact Point (NCP). Free, government-funded advisers for Horizon Europe in each country. They are good for interpreting an ESR or a letter. They won't write or manage your grant for you, and response times vary by country.
  • Private grant consultant. Some handle resubmission rewrites and grant preparation for a fee or a success fee. Fees vary widely, so ask for a written quote and check it against the official rules (as of October 2026; check the provider's own page). A consultant suits a team with no grant office facing a tight resubmission date. It makes less sense for a university that already has a research office, and no consultant can change scores or speed up the Commission's timeline.
  • For technical problems (missing documents, withdrawal after the deadline), use the portal's free IT Helpdesk. Don't hire anyone for that.

Related guides on this site:

  • Horizon Europe Proposal Template Part B: 2026 Scoring Map
  • EU Funding for SMEs: 7 Open 2026 Calls and How to Qualify
  • Cascade Funding Open Calls: Portal Filters and 2026 Dates

FAQ

Why does my proposal status still say 'under evaluation' after the expected date?

The 5-month and 3-month figures are approximate ("around"), and calls with very large numbers of proposals often run late. The status in the list may not change until a letter is posted in Follow-up > Documents, so check there rather than relying on the list view. If you're well past the topic's stated date, ask the IT Helpdesk or the call's functional mailbox listed on the topic page.

What is the difference between 'ineligible' and 'below threshold'?

An ineligible (or inadmissible) proposal failed formal checks, such as an incomplete application or a consortium that doesn't meet the rules. It was never scored (Admissibility and eligibility check). A below-threshold proposal was scored by experts but missed a criterion threshold or the overall threshold. Both can be challenged through redress within 30 days, but only on procedural grounds.

Can I edit a proposal after the submission deadline?

No. "It will not be possible to edit proposals for calls which are already closed" (Submit). You keep read-only access to the submitted version. The only thing you can request after the deadline is a withdrawal, through the IT Helpdesk.

What does 'redress procedure' mean in the evaluation result?

It is a formal request to review the admissibility, eligibility or evaluation process. You file it within 30 days of receiving your letter, using Launch new interaction with the EU > Launch Redress Case. The text is limited to 7,000 characters, in plain text with no links (Redress). Valid grounds include procedural irregularities, factual errors or comments that contradict the scores. Each proposal gets one request, and it can't be edited once submitted (Complaints about proposal rejection).
