item.title: EU Funding and Tenders Portal Two Factor Authentication 2026
item.dc:creator: Aoba Works
item.description: EU Funding and Tenders Portal two factor authentication setup: EU Login app, passkey and security key in 5 steps, plus lost-phone recovery and fixes for 2026.
item.content:encoded:
How this guide was made: drafted with AI assistance from the official sources linked below, then passed an automated editorial check before publishing. Our process

To pass two-factor authentication on the EU Funding and Tenders Portal, you add a second verification method to your EU Login account. The options are the EU Login Mobile App, a passkey, a security key, a "trusted platform" (the security chip already in your computer) or a national eID. Then you switch 2FA on under Security Settings. SMS codes no longer count, because EU Login phased them out on 30 June 2025. Since the 2026 rollout, the Commission has made 2FA mandatory for all Portal users, so you need it working before you can submit a proposal or manage a PIC.

Which option is right for you?

For most readers, the EU Login Mobile App plus one backup method is the best start. The table matches each situation to a method and the first page to open.

Your situationWhat to pick firstFirst page to open
Beginner with a smartphone (Android 7.0+ or iOS 12+)EU Login Mobile App with a 4-digit PINEU Login → My Account → Manage my mobile devices
Daily work at the same office PC (grant office, LEAR, consultant)App first, then a trusted platform (Windows Hello / Mac Secure Enclave) as a fast backupManage my Trusted Platforms, Security Keys and Passkeys
No budget and no smartphoneTrusted platform or a passkey in a password manager you already useManage my Trusted Platforms, Security Keys and Passkeys → Add a passkey
You move between many computers or remote desktopsA FIDO2 security key (a one-off hardware purchase)Add a security key
You already use a national digital IDeID, where your country supports itManage my eID
You lost your only deviceThe PANIC reset, then register againMy Account → Delete all my devices and eID (PANIC)

Why these picks: the Commission recommends the app because it supports biometrics and an offline QR code. A built-in trusted platform costs nothing. A security key is the only option that travels with you and doesn't depend on a phone battery.

What is EU Login and why does the Funding & Tenders Portal require two-factor authentication?

EU Login is the European Commission's shared sign-in service, and the Funding & Tenders Portal requires 2FA on it because Portal accounts control proposals, grant signatures and legal-entity data.

The Portal has no password system of its own. When you click Login on the Portal, you are sent to EU Login (webgate.ec.europa.eu/cas), and the same account works for other Commission services. Your 2FA settings live in EU Login, not in the Portal. That is why every setup step below happens under My Account in EU Login.

The Commission's stated aim is to "increase the level of data and account protection". The risk is concrete. A Portal account can submit a proposal on behalf of a consortium, accept a grant agreement or change an organisation's bank and legal data. When EU Login dropped SMS, it pointed to "phishing, SIM swapping, and message interception".

Example: suppose a research officer's password leaks through an unrelated website breach. Without 2FA, anyone holding that password could open the officer's draft proposals. With 2FA, the attacker would also need the officer's phone, security key or computer chip.

Pitfalls:

  • Treating the Portal and EU Login as separate accounts. If you created two EU Login accounts (for example, a personal Gmail one and a work one), 2FA on one does not protect the other. Your Portal roles stay tied to whichever email they were given to.
  • Assuming SMS still works. Old university guides still describe "Mobile Phone + SMS". That method was disabled by 30 June 2025.

How to set up two-factor authentication on EU Login step by step

You set up 2FA in EU Login under My Account: register one verification method, activate 2FA in Security Settings, then answer three security questions. The five steps below use the EU Login Mobile App, which is the Commission's recommended method. They follow the official installation guide and the Portal's IT How To page.

Before you start, have two devices ready: a computer with internet access and a phone or tablet. The phone must have a screen lock (PIN or biometrics). You will also need to allow the app to use the camera and send notifications (source). The minimum versions are Android 7.0 and iOS/iPadOS 12.0 (source).

Step 1: Install the app

  1. Install EU Login from Google Play or the App Store. Check that the publisher is the European Commission.
  2. Open it. On the Welcome screen, tap Link device to my account. The app then shows an overview of the registration steps.

Step 2: Open your account settings on the computer

  1. Go to https://ecas.ec.europa.eu/cas and sign in with your email and password.
  2. Click the cogwheel icon (or your profile avatar) and choose My Account.
  3. Select Manage my mobile devices, then Add a mobile device.

Step 3: Name the device and set a PIN

  1. Enter a device name without spaces. For example, Pixel8-work works but My work phone does not.
  2. Choose a 4-digit PIN and confirm it. You will type this PIN on the phone at every login unless you turn on biometrics.
  3. Submit. A QR code appears in the browser.

Step 4: Link the phone

  1. On the phone, tap Continue and scan the QR code on the computer screen.
  2. Enter the 4-digit PIN from Step 3.
  3. Optionally turn on fingerprint, face recognition or Face ID. You can skip this and enable it later in the app's settings.
  4. Tap Finish registration.

Step 5: Activate 2FA and set your security questions

  1. Back in My Account, open Security Settings and click Activate.
  2. Set up three security questions. Use Latin characters only and no special characters (source). Click Send Questions.

Write the answers down somewhere safe, such as a password manager note. These three answers are what let you remove or replace a lost method later. Without them, you have to contact the helpdesk.

Example of a login afterwards: you enter your password on the Portal, choose EU Login Mobile App PIN Code, and approve the notification on your phone with your PIN or fingerprint. If the phone has no data signal, choose the QR code option instead and scan the code from the screen.

Common mistakes and fixes:

  • Space in the device name → the form rejects it. Use hyphens.
  • Camera permission denied → the QR scan fails silently. Allow camera access for EU Login in the phone settings and scan again.
  • Accents or symbols in the security answers ("Zürich", "O'Brien") → they break the Latin-characters rule. Use plain letters.

Which 2FA methods does EU Login support (authenticator app vs SMS vs EU Login Mobile app)?

EU Login supports its own Mobile App, passkeys, FIDO2 security keys, trusted platforms and national eID. SMS has been withdrawn, and generic authenticator apps such as Google Authenticator are not on the official list.

So the "authenticator app vs SMS" choice many people search for does not exist here. The real choice is between the methods in this table.

MethodWhat you needStrengthsLimitationsNot for
EU Login Mobile App (PIN or QR)Smartphone/tablet, Android 7.0+ / iOS 12+Recommended by the Commission. Biometrics. The QR mode works offlineMust be re-linked after a phone change or app reinstall (source)People without a personal or work smartphone
Trusted platformPC with a TPM chip or Mac with Secure EnclaveFree. Uses your normal Windows/Mac sign-inWorks only on that one computerHot-desking staff, shared PCs
Security keyFIDO2 USB/NFC/Bluetooth keyPortable. Phishing-resistant. No batteryOne-off hardware cost (check vendor prices). Can be lostAnyone who works only on a phone
Passkey (password manager or phone)Bitwarden, Dashlane, Proton Pass, LastPass, RoboForm, NordPass or Keeper (official list), or a phoneSyncs across devicesThe Commission notes that a cloud-stored private key is "less secured". Phone-based passkeys need Bluetooth on both devicesUsers whose IT policy blocks browser extensions
National eIDA supported national eID (e.g. itsme in Belgium)No extra device if you already use itCountry-specificNon-EU users and countries not connected
SMS——Disabled by 30 June 2025Everyone

To add any method other than the app, go to My Account → Manage my Trusted Platforms, Security Keys and Passkeys. Then pick Add a Trusted Platform, Add a security key or Add a passkey, enter a device name and click Submit (source). With a security key, you touch the key when prompted. With a trusted platform, your computer asks for its usual PIN or fingerprint.

Which one to pick: if you have a smartphone, register the app first, because it covers almost every case. Then add the trusted platform on the computer you submit proposals from. Your backup is then free and needs no setup on the day you lose your phone.

Pitfalls:

  • Passkey limits: you can store one passkey per EU Login account per device (source).
  • Remote desktop: password-manager passkeys only work there if you can install the browser extension and the session has internet access (source).
  • Adding a second method may ask for your first one. Adding a method "may require stronger authentication" once you already have a second factor, so keep the first device nearby.

How to recover access if you lose your 2FA device or phone number

If you lose your device, sign in with another registered method or answer your security questions to replace it. If you have nothing else, external self-registered users can wipe all methods with the PANIC button and start again.

Which path applies depends on what you set up beforehand.

Path A: you have a second registered method

  1. Sign in with the backup method (trusted platform, security key or passkey).
  2. Go to My Account → Manage my mobile devices and delete the lost device.
  3. Add the new phone using Steps 1–4 above (source).

Path B: no other method, but you know your security questions

The Portal's IT guide says you can replace the method by answering your three questions. If 2FA is not mandatory for your account, you can also deactivate it this way (source).

Path C: the PANIC button (external self-registered accounts)

This follows the official EU Login help article:

  1. Clear your browser cookies.
  2. Open My Account and sign in with your email and password only.
  3. Click Delete all my devices and eID (PANIC).
  4. Confirm with Delete. You get a confirmation message and are logged out.
  5. Sign in again and register a new method straight away.

PANIC removes every phone, device, hardware token and eID linked to the account. The button only appears once at least one 2FA method is registered.

Path D: nothing works

If you forgot the security questions, or you have an EU institution staff account, you need to request a reset. Use the Portal helpdesk contact form and select EU Login as the domain and Two-Factor Authentication as the category (source). For EU Login itself, write to EU-LOGIN-EXTERNAL-SUPPORT@ec.europa.eu (source).

Pitfalls:

  • Losing the phone in the week of a deadline. The Commission does not publish a turnaround time for helpdesk resets, so don't plan around one. A free trusted-platform backup avoids the problem.
  • "Always require multi-factor authentication". If you turned this setting on and then lose all factors, the password-only route disappears and you must contact support (source).

How to add or change a mobile phone number for EU Login authentication

Changing your phone number no longer affects EU Login 2FA, because SMS codes were withdrawn. What matters is the device: a new phone has to be linked again in Manage my mobile devices.

Older guides describe Manage my mobile phone numbers under My Account for external users (example guide). That screen was for the SMS method, which ended by 30 June 2025. A new SIM in the same handset has no effect on the app. A new handset is what breaks the link.

When you get a new phone (old phone still working)

  1. Install the EU Login app on the new phone.
  2. Sign in on the computer and go to My Account → Manage my mobile devices.
  3. Choose Add a mobile device. EU Login asks you to confirm with the old device or another registered method (source).
  4. Finish linking the new phone, then delete the old entry.

Do this before you wipe or trade in the old phone. Otherwise you are on the PANIC path described above.

Pitfalls:

  • Restoring from a backup and expecting the app to carry over. It won't: the app must be re-registered after a reset or device change.
  • Sharing one phone between colleagues. The current official guide says the app now supports multiple accounts. An older Commission page states one account per device, though. If a second account won't link, give that person a passkey or security key instead.

What to do when EU Login two-factor authentication is not working

Most 2FA failures come from a device that was never linked or was reset, missing permissions, stale cookies, or the wrong account. You can fix each of these without a full reset.

Go through this table before you contact the helpdesk.

SymptomLikely causeFix
Error 5305 when logging in with the appThe app is installed but not linked to this accountMy Account → Manage my mobile devices → Add a mobile device (FAQ)
No push notification arrivesNotifications blocked or no data connectionAllow notifications for EU Login, or choose the QR code method, which works offline
QR scan does nothingCamera permission offEnable camera access for the app and rescan
App asks to register again after an update or reinstallThe device link was lostDelete the old device under Manage my mobile devices and add it again (source)
"You are currently logged in as user 'n00xxxx' and cannot use an authentication factor registered to user…"You are signed in to a different EU Login accountFollow the reconciliation process
The password option is missing at login"Always require multi-factor authentication" is on, or the application restricts itUse a registered factor, or contact support if you have none
Login loops back to the start pageOld session cookiesClear cookies for ec.europa.eu, then sign in again

Example: a consultant installs the EU Login app on a new phone and tries to log in at once. The Portal shows error 5305. The fix is to link the phone first under Add a mobile device, confirming with the old phone. If the old phone is gone, use PANIC.

The Commission also published a one-page 2FA infographic covering eight common situations, including device loss and error 5305. It ran a practical webinar on 13 May 2026 (source). Keep the infographic open while you troubleshoot.

Pitfall: don't delete and reinstall the app as your first move. If the app is your only method, a reinstall cuts the link, and you end up on the PANIC path.

How does EU Login 2FA affect PIC registration and organisation account setup on the Funding & Tenders Portal

Every Portal login now needs 2FA, so the person registering the organisation, and later the LEAR, must set up 2FA before starting PIC registration. Without it, they can't reach the Participant Register.

The Online Manual still says you only need an EU Login account to start registering. It doesn't mention 2FA, because it was written before the rollout. In practice, the order is now:

  1. Create the EU Login account with a work email. All Portal roles attach to that address.
  2. Set up 2FA (the five steps above) and add a backup method.
  3. Register the organisation in the Participant Register to get the 9-digit PIC. It starts as provisional, "declared/non-valid status". Our PIC registration guide covers this part in six steps.
  4. Validation and LEAR appointment. Validation must come first; the LEAR is appointed after it (LEAR page). The LEAR also needs their own EU Login account with 2FA.
  5. Assign Account Administrators and signatories. Every person the LEAR adds will hit the same 2FA prompt on their first login.

Example: a five-person startup preparing an EIC Accelerator application. The founder self-registers the company, and the CFO becomes LEAR after validation. If the CFO's only factor is the app on a phone they are about to replace, the company's single LEAR could be locked out just before grant signature. Having each of them add a trusted platform as well removes that risk.

Pitfalls:

  • Registering the PIC under a personal email and then moving to a work email. The roles stay on the old account, along with its 2FA.
  • Leaving 2FA setup for submission day. Partners in a consortium all need working access to the proposal. If you're coordinating a two-stage health call such as HORIZON-HLTH-2027-02-TOOL-01, ask every partner contact to confirm their 2FA when the consortium forms.

Is two-factor authentication mandatory for all EU Login users or only certain roles

Yes, it is mandatory for all Funding & Tenders Portal users, not only LEARs or signatories. The Commission rolled it out in batches and finished on 30 June 2026.

The Portal's IT guide states that 2FA becomes mandatory for all users during 2026. The timeline as of October 2026:

DateWhat happenedSource
30 June 2025SMS second factor disabledF&T Portal news
10 December 2025Pilot of mandatory 2FA starts with expert evaluatorsMMU research blog, Portal news for experts
January–June 2026Gradual rollout by batches, with users notified individuallyUKRO update
20 April 2026Users without 2FA asked to set it up on first loginUniversity of Siena
30 June 2026Portal access only after 2FA verificationUKRO update

The scope is wide: researchers, evaluators and organisation staff in any EU programme. Browsing calls without signing in is still open to everyone, so you can search for SME calls without an account. 2FA starts the moment you click Login.

Pitfall: other Commission applications that use EU Login have their own rules. A service that still accepts your password alone doesn't mean the Portal will. Set 2FA up once at account level and it covers both.

Next steps

Today, you can finish the setup and add a backup method on your own in under an hour. If you'd rather have help, free official support comes first.

DIY actions for today:

  1. Install the EU Login app and complete the five setup steps, including the three security questions.
  2. Add a second method under Manage my Trusted Platforms, Security Keys and Passkeys. The trusted platform on your main computer is free.
  3. If you are a LEAR or self-registrant, confirm that your Portal roles sit on the same work-email account that now has 2FA. Then ask each Account Administrator to do the same.

If you'd rather not do it yourself:

  • Commission helpdesk and infographic (free). The contact form and the 2FA infographic suit anyone who is stuck. The limitation: no published response time, so they're not a deadline-day rescue.
  • Your National Contact Point or university research office (usually free to applicants). Good if you're new to the Portal. They can't reset your EU Login, though; only the Commission can.
  • Paid grant consultant. Fees vary widely and are usually charged as part of proposal support (as of October 2026; check each provider's terms). This makes sense if you're buying help with the proposal itself, such as Part B scoring. Paying someone only for 2FA setup is poor value. Also, never give a consultant your EU Login password or device: the account is personal and tied to your legal role.

Related guides on this site:

  • EU Funding and Tenders Portal Registration: PIC in 6 Steps
  • EU Funding for SMEs: 7 Open 2026 Calls and How to Qualify
  • Cascade Funding Open Calls: Portal Filters and 2026 Dates

FAQ

Can I use the same EU Login 2FA setup for other EU portals besides Funding & Tenders?

Yes. 2FA is set on your EU Login account, not on the Portal, so any Commission service that signs you in through EU Login uses the same registered methods. Some services restrict which methods they accept, so a method that works on the Portal may be refused elsewhere (source).

What happens if my organisation's LEAR changes and loses 2FA access?

A LEAR's 2FA is personal and can't be handed over. If the LEAR is still with the organisation but has lost their device, they recover through a backup method, the security questions, PANIC or the helpdesk. If the LEAR has left, the organisation appoints a new one through the LEAR appointment procedure. The new LEAR then sets up 2FA on their own EU Login account.

Does EU Login 2FA work without a smartphone?

Yes. You can use a trusted platform (a PC with a TPM chip or a Mac with Secure Enclave), a FIDO2 security key, a passkey stored in a password manager, or a national eID where available (source). SMS on a basic phone is no longer an option.

How long does EU Login account recovery take after losing 2FA access?

With a backup method or PANIC, recovery is immediate: you remove the old device and register a new one in the same session (source). If you need a helpdesk reset because you forgot your security questions, there is no published turnaround time. Set up a backup method well before any call deadline.

item.title: HORIZON-HLTH-2027-02-TOOL-01-two-stage: Dates & Page Limits
item.dc:creator: Aoba Works
item.description: HORIZON-HLTH-2027-02-TOOL-01-two-stage: 17 Feb and 16 Sep 2027 deadlines, 10- vs 40-page limits, scoring thresholds and portal steps for AI biomarkers.
item.content:encoded:
How this guide was made: drafted with AI assistance from the official sources linked below, then passed an automated editorial check before publishing. Our process

HORIZON-HLTH-2027-02-TOOL-01-two-stage is a Horizon Europe Health call for AI methods that predict how chronic non-communicable diseases progress and how patients respond to treatment. It opens on 29 October 2026. The Stage 1 deadline is 17 February 2027 and the Stage 2 deadline is 16 September 2027, both at 17:00 Brussels time (Accelopment summary of the official Work Programme; Institut Pasteur). To apply, you submit a 10-page anonymised outline that is scored on Excellence and Impact. If you pass, you are invited to submit a full proposal that is also scored on Implementation. The topic has a budget of EUR 44.2 million, enough for about six projects of EUR 6–8 million each (portal topic data).

Which option is right for you?

The best first step depends on your role. A clinical or academic group should open the topic page, a company should look at how it fits the consortium, and a newcomer should register first.

Your situationWhat to pick firstFirst page to open
First-time applicant (no PIC, never submitted)Register your organisation, then join an existing consortium as a partner instead of coordinatingPIC registration guide
University hospital or research institute with cohort dataCoordinate or lead the validation work package. Prospective clinical studies must be led from the EU/EFTA or an Associated CountryTopic data on the portal
AI/health-tech SME or startupJoin as a partner and own the exploitation and decision-support tool. SMEs are explicitly encouragedEU funding for SMEs
SME with a product close to market and no consortiumThis call is probably the wrong fit. Look at single-company instrumentsEIC Accelerator deadlines
Small budget, want a smaller grantCascade (third-party) funding calls are lighter to apply forCascade funding open calls
Grant consultant or project officerStart from the scoring map and the blind-evaluation rulesPart B scoring map

Coordinating is a heavy job: you manage the Stage 1 submission and then the full proposal over about seven months. If you have never done it before, being a partner is the safer first role.

What is HORIZON-HLTH-2027-02-TOOL-01 about?

The topic funds work that uses established AI methods to find, validate and deploy predictive biomarkers for chronic non-communicable diseases. Cancer is excluded (portal topic data). The full title is "Development of predictive biomarkers of disease progression and treatment response by using AI methodologies for chronic non-communicable diseases". It is a Research and Innovation Action (HORIZON-RIA).

The official text lists four expected outcomes. Paraphrased:

  1. Clinical researchers get access to novel predictive biomarkers for assessing disease progression and treatment response more accurately.
  2. Clinicians use clinically validated predictive biomarkers in clinical research and personalised medicine.
  3. Stakeholders get trustworthy AI tools that guide the development of multimodal predictive biomarkers.
  4. Citizens benefit from better clinical guidelines and biomarker-guided clinical research.

The scope then asks for five activities. Reviewers will look for each of them:

  • Map what exists. Set up a multidisciplinary collaboration that maps and evaluates the biomarker data already used in clinics. Include stratification by biological sex and, where feasible, gender-related and sociodemographic variables.
  • Adapt, don't invent. The text says to "adapt and apply established AI methods rather than developing novel ones from scratch". These methods should run on multimodal biomarkers (molecular, cellular, physiological, imaging, behavioural, digital) combined with longitudinal clinical studies and real-world data (RWD).
  • Model relationships with trustworthy AI. Describe how biomarkers relate to each other, with a focus on AI trustworthiness, plus "user-friendly and fit-for-purpose visualisation and decision-support tools".
  • Validate clinically. Build a biomarker validation platform and run validation studies in independent disease cohorts, RWD and exploratory clinical studies.
  • Plan exploitation and regulation. Write an exploitation plan and a regulatory strategy, with priority on exploiting results in the EU.

On top of these five, projects must follow GDPR-compliant data protection practice. They are encouraged to use research and data infrastructures funded under the Digital Europe Programme. They should also set aside budget for networking and joint activities with other funded projects (portal topic data).

Example (illustrative only): a consortium working on chronic kidney disease could pool longitudinal registry data, proteomics and wearable data from three national cohorts. It would fine-tune existing gradient-boosting and survival models, then validate the predicted progression risk in a fourth cohort it did not train on. The tool would be a clinician dashboard. A proposal like this matches all five activities. A proposal built around a new foundation model architecture does not match the second one.

What is the deadline for Stage 1 and Stage 2?

Stage 1 closes on 17 February 2027 and Stage 2 on 16 September 2027, both at 17:00 Brussels local time. The call opens on 29 October 2026 (Accelopment, reporting the Work Programme published on 1 October 2026).

MilestoneDate (as of October 2026)Who submits
Call opens29 October 2026—
Stage 1 deadline17 February 2027, 17:00 BrusselsAny eligible consortium
Stage 2 deadline16 September 2027, 17:00 BrusselsOnly consortia invited after Stage 1

These dates are newer than the draft dates. The draft Work Programme had the call opening on 10 February 2027, with Stage 1 on 13 April 2027 and Stage 2 on 22 September 2027. The final version moved everything earlier (Accelopment on the draft changes). Some third-party pages still show the old April dates, for example this tips page. Plan around 17 February. The Work Programme also lets the responsible Director-General delay deadlines by up to two months (Institut Pasteur summary). Don't build your plan on that possibility.

One trap: as of 22 October 2026 the topic status on the portal is "Forthcoming". The topic data feed we read still showed placeholder dates (June and September 2026) that don't match the Work Programme (portal topic data). Once the call opens, the deadline shown in the Submission service is the one that counts.

What are the page limits for Stage 1 vs Stage 2?

Stage 1 has a 10-page limit. A full Stage 2 RIA proposal has a 40-page limit, or 45 pages if the topic uses lump-sum funding (General Annexes 2026-2027; summarised by criteri.ai). The topic conditions we read don't mention lump sums (portal topic data), so 40 pages is the likely limit. Confirm it in the Stage 2 template, which is generated for the topic.

Stage 1Stage 2
Part B page limit10 pages40 pages (45 if lump sum)
SectionsExcellence, ImpactExcellence, Impact, Implementation
AnonymityBlind: no organisation names, logos or staff names in abstract or Part BNot blind
Clinical studies annexCheck the Stage 1 templateRequired: details in the dedicated annex template (portal)
Template versionDownload from the Submission serviceStandard Application Form (HE RIA/IA) V5.x, from the Submission service

The 2026–2027 application form (V5.0 from November 2025, V5.1 from January 2026) reduced the page allowance and simplified sections 2.1 and 3.1 (criteri.ai, citing the official version history; Accelopment on template changes). Old Part B files from 2024 calls should only be used for reference.

Common pitfalls and fixes:

  • Going over the limit. Evaluators ignore pages beyond the limit. Fix: freeze the outline at 9 pages a week before the deadline, which leaves room for late edits.
  • Identifying yourself in Stage 1. First-stage proposals in the 2026–27 programme are evaluated blind. Part A data is hidden automatically, but removing names from Part B and the abstract is your job, and a direct identification makes the proposal inadmissible (summary of General Annexes rules). Fix: write "Partner 1 (university hospital, 4,000-patient CKD cohort)" and never "Charité cohort". Also remove named software, grant numbers and self-citations that reveal who you are.
  • Using the wrong template. Fix: download Part B from inside your draft in the Submission service, not from an old shared drive.

Who can apply to this call (eligibility)?

Under the standard Horizon Europe RIA rule in the General Annexes, you need at least three independent legal entities from three different EU Member States or Associated Countries, with at least one in a Member State. The topic adds one rule of its own: prospective clinical studies must be led by entities in the EU/EFTA and/or Associated Countries (portal topic data; General Annexes). The topic refers to Annex B of the General Annexes for eligible countries and Annex C for financial and operational capacity.

US entities can receive funding here. The Health cluster opens Union funding to US-based legal entities in recognition of NIH funding European researchers (Science|Business on EU–NIH reciprocity). Check the "Conditions" section on the topic page once the call opens to confirm this still applies. Partners from other non-associated countries usually join at their own cost.

Steps to check eligibility before you write anything:

  1. List every partner with its country and legal status (university, hospital, SME, NGO, public body).
  2. Confirm that at least three are independent of each other and based in three different EU/Associated countries.
  3. Mark which partner leads each prospective clinical study and confirm it is EU/EFTA/Associated-based.
  4. Make sure every partner has a 9-digit PIC. If not, follow the PIC registration guide.
  5. Check whether your coordinator is likely to pass the financial capacity check (Annex C). Coordinators of grants of EUR 6–8 million get the most scrutiny.

Pitfall: two hospital departments of the same university group count as one entity if they are not independent. Fix: add a separate entity from a third country.

What is the evaluation criteria for Stage 1?

At Stage 1, experts score only Excellence and Impact, and each criterion needs at least 4 out of 5 (portal topic data). That is stricter than the usual full-proposal threshold of 3, and the bar can rise further.

The General Annexes also set an overall threshold on the sum of the two scores. It is chosen so that the total budget requested by proposals going to Stage 2 is close to three times the available budget, and never less than twice. In practice it is "expected normally to be set at 8 or 8.5" (General Annexes rules, as summarised).

Stage 1 elementRule
CriteriaExcellence, Impact (aspects narrower than in a full proposal; see General Annexes Section D)
Individual threshold4/5 each
Overall thresholdSet after submission; normally 8 or 8.5 out of 10
Evaluation modeBlind
Funnel targetRequested budget of invited proposals around 3× the EUR 44.2M available

With EUR 44.2 million available, that funnel means roughly EUR 130 million of proposals reach Stage 2, or about 16–22 consortia at EUR 6–8 million each (example arithmetic, not an official figure). For about six grants, that works out to around one in three invited proposals being funded.

What scores 4+ at Stage 1 for this topic, based on the scope:

  • A named disease area (or a clearly argued cluster of NCDs) and a clear gap in current predictive biomarkers.
  • Evidence you have the data: cohort sizes, follow-up length, data types, and an independent validation cohort. Describe these without naming the institutions.
  • An explicit statement that you adapt established AI methods, with the trustworthiness and bias work you will do.
  • A credible route to clinical use: guidelines, regulatory strategy, and exploitation in the EU.

For section-by-section scoring prompts, use the Part B scoring map.

What is the evaluation criteria for Stage 2?

At Stage 2, experts score Excellence, Impact and Implementation. Each needs at least 4 out of 5, and the total must reach 12 out of 15 (portal topic data). Generic guides often quote the standard 3/5 per criterion and 10/15 overall. Those numbers do not apply to this topic.

CriterionThresholdWhat carries weight for this topic
Excellence4/5Methodology for multimodal data integration, validation design in independent cohorts, sex/gender stratification, AI trustworthiness
Impact4/5Pathways to the four expected outcomes, regulatory strategy, exploitation in the EU, GDPR-compliant data practice
Implementation4/5Work plan, clinical studies annex, consortium roles (clinical lead in EU/EFTA/AC), resources, networking budget
Total12/15Above the threshold, projects are ranked against each other for the EUR 44.2M

Stage 2 must build on what you promised at Stage 1. If you change the objectives a lot, reviewers will notice a mismatch with the outline they invited. You can strengthen the consortium, for example by adding an SME for the decision-support tool, as long as the core concept stays the same.

Pitfalls and fixes at Stage 2:

  • Treating the clinical studies annex as optional. The topic requires it (portal). Fix: draft it in parallel with the work plan, starting in spring 2027.
  • No budget for networking. The scope asks for "sufficient budget for networking and joint activities". Fix: put a specific person-month and travel line in a work package.
  • A vague regulatory plan. Fix: name the regulatory route your tool would likely follow and when you plan to engage regulators.

How do I submit a proposal via the Funding & Tenders Portal?

You submit from the topic page by clicking "Start submission". This opens the Submission wizard, where you create the draft, add partners, complete Part A and upload Part B before 17:00 Brussels time (Online Manual: Electronic proposal submission; IT How To: Submit a proposal).

  1. Create an EU Login account for every person who will edit the proposal.
  2. Get a PIC for each organisation in the Participant Register (step-by-step guide).
  3. Find the topic. On the Funding & Tenders Portal, go to "Search Funding & Tenders" and search for HORIZON-HLTH-2027-02-TOOL-01-two-stage. The "Start submission" button appears once the status changes from "Forthcoming" to "Open" (expected 29 October 2026).
  4. Click "Start submission" and choose the action type HORIZON-RIA when asked.
  5. Pre-register the draft. The coordinator enters the acronym and short summary. Keep the summary anonymous, because it is also covered by blind evaluation.
  6. Add participants. In the participants step, add each partner by PIC and give contact persons their access roles.
  7. Complete Part A (the administrative forms): budget table, declarations, ethics and security self-assessment.
  8. Download the Part B template from inside the draft, write it, export it to PDF and upload it.
  9. Click "Validate" and fix every error the system flags (missing fields, page count, file format).
  10. Click "Submit" and check that you receive the acknowledgement of receipt. You can resubmit as often as you want before the deadline. Only the last version is evaluated.

For Stage 2, only invited coordinators can open the second-stage draft. Partners and Part A data are carried over and you can edit them.

Common mistakes:

  • Submitting at 16:55. The portal is busy on deadline day. Fix: submit a complete version 48 hours early, then overwrite it if needed.
  • Partners without PICs on deadline week. Fix: collect PICs in November 2026, well before the deadline.
  • Identifying metadata in the PDF. File properties can contain author names. Fix: clear the document properties before exporting.

What is the indicative budget and project duration for this call?

The topic budget is EUR 44.20 million for 2027, with an expected EU contribution of EUR 6–8 million per project and about six grants (portal topic data; Accelopment). The topic text we read sets no fixed duration, so you choose one and justify it in the work plan.

ItemFigure (as of October 2026)
Topic budgetEUR 44.20 million
EU contribution per projectEUR 6.00–8.00 million
Expected number of grantsAbout 6
Type of actionRIA (normally 100% of eligible costs funded)
DurationNot set in topic. Justify it in your work plan

Because this is an RIA, the EU normally reimburses 100% of eligible costs, plus a 25% flat rate for indirect costs (General Annexes). You can ask for more than EUR 8 million, but "the range" signals what evaluators expect. A request far outside it has to be argued clearly.

Example budget split (illustrative, not official guidance): for a EUR 7 million request over 48 months, a consortium might put about 40% into clinical validation (cohort access, exploratory studies), 25% into AI modelling and trustworthiness, 15% into the decision-support tool and its usability, 10% into exploitation and regulation, and 10% into management, dissemination and networking. Validation-heavy splits like this match the scope's weight on clinical utility.

AI-driven biomarkers vs traditional biomarkers: what does this call expect?

The call wants established AI/ML methods applied to multimodal data and validated clinically. A single-marker study using classic statistics doesn't fit, and neither does inventing a new AI architecture (portal topic data). The difference is real, and many proposals get it wrong in one direction or the other.

AspectTraditional biomarker projectWhat TOOL-01 expects
DataOne modality (e.g., a serum protein)Multimodal: molecular, cellular, physiological, imaging, behavioural, digital markers + longitudinal clinical data + RWD
MethodsHypothesis-driven statisticsEstablished AI methods, adapted, plus other data-integration methods where needed
NoveltyNew marker discoveryPredictive value from combining and relating markers. New AI methods "from scratch" are discouraged
TrustAnalytical validityAI trustworthiness, bias assessment, sex/gender stratification
OutputPaper, assayValidation platform, decision-support and visualisation tools, regulatory strategy
ValidationOften internalIndependent disease cohorts, RWD and exploratory clinical studies

Example of fit (illustrative): a Parkinson's disease project that combines digital gait data from smartphones, MRI and CSF markers, uses existing deep survival models, and checks performance separately for women and men. This matches the topic. A project whose main deliverable is a new transformer architecture for omics belongs elsewhere. The 2027 Health programme has a separate topic, HORIZON-HLTH-2027-03-TOOL-08, on frontier AI models for healthcare (Accelopment).

Pitfalls:

  • "AI-washing". Mentioning machine learning without saying which models, which data and which validation metric. Fix: name the model family, the training and validation cohorts, and the clinical endpoint.
  • Cancer creeping in. Cancer is out of scope. Fix: keep oncology comorbidities out of your main endpoints.
  • No plan for clinicians to use it. Fix: put usability testing of the decision-support tool with clinicians into a work package.

Next steps

You can start today, three and a half months before the Stage 1 deadline. Here is what to do yourself, what you could hand off, and where to read next.

Do it yourself today:

  1. Check the PIC of every likely partner and ask anyone without one to register this week (guide).
  2. Write a one-page anonymised concept that covers the disease area, data modalities, cohort sizes, independent validation cohort and the clinical decision your tool supports. Test it against the five scope activities above.
  3. Put 29 October 2026 (call opens), 17 February 2027 and 16 September 2027 in your shared calendar, with an internal Stage 1 submission date of 13 February.

If you'd rather not do it alone:

  • National Contact Points (NCPs) for Cluster 1 Health are free, official advisers in each country. They review eligibility and explain the rules (Health NCP network). They suit first-time coordinators. They are not ghost-writers: they won't write your Part B, and how much time they can give varies by country.
  • Private grant consultancies can write or edit proposals for a fee. Ask for a written quote that sets out the full fee structure before you commit. They suit consortia that have strong science but little proposal-writing time. They are a poor fit if you can't share confidential data or can't afford fees on a call where most applicants are not funded. A consultant still can't create a validation cohort you don't have.

Related guides on this site:

  • Horizon Europe Proposal Template Part B: 2026 Scoring Map
  • EU Funding for SMEs: 7 Open 2026 Calls and How to Qualify
  • EIC Accelerator Deadlines: 2026 Cut-Off Dates and Steps
  • Cascade Funding Open Calls: Portal Filters and 2026 Dates

FAQ

What are common reasons proposals get rejected at Stage 1?

The usual reasons are missing the 4/5 threshold on Excellence or Impact, or landing under an overall cut-off that is normally 8 or 8.5. For this topic, typical weak points are no independent validation cohort, proposing new AI methods instead of adapting established ones, and no sex/gender stratification. Identifying your organisation in Part B or the abstract breaks the blind-evaluation rule and can make the proposal inadmissible.

Can a project resubmit if not invited to Stage 2?

Nothing in the topic text bars you from submitting an improved version to a later suitable call. But this topic appears only in the 2027 call of the 2026–2027 Work Programme, so there is no second cut-off for it. Use the evaluation feedback to rework the idea for another Health topic, and check each new call's own rules.

Does this call require patient data management plans?

The topic requires GDPR-compliant personal data protection and AI and datasets that comply with privacy-preserving law (portal topic data). The standard RIA Part B also asks how you will manage research data (annotated RIA/IA template). At Stage 2 you also complete the clinical studies annex, which covers how patient data are collected and handled.

Is there a specific TRL (Technology Readiness Level) requirement?

No. The topic conditions we read do not set a TRL. Because this is an RIA with clinical validation and exploratory studies, evaluators will expect the project to move biomarkers and tools from proven concept towards clinically tested prototypes. Describe the starting point and the end point clearly in the Excellence section.

item.title: Cascade Funding Open Calls: Portal Filters and 2026 Dates
item.dc:creator: Aoba Works
item.description: Find cascade funding open calls on the EU Funding & Tenders Portal: exact filter steps, the €60,000 FSTP cap, and key 2026 deadlines to track.
item.content:encoded:
How this guide was made: drafted with AI assistance from the official sources linked below, then passed an automated editorial check before publishing. Our process

You can find cascade funding open calls on the EU Funding & Tenders Portal. Open Calls for proposals, go to the Type of grants calls filter and select "Calls for funding in cascade (issued by funded projects)", then remove closed calls (EC IT How To; BAYFOR). The Portal shows the title, opening date and deadline of each call. Grant sizes, eligibility and the application form are only on the website of the project running the call, so plan to open two tabs for every call.

Which option is right for you?

Your starting point depends on how much time you have and whether you want a small, quick sub-grant or a full EU grant.

Your situationWhat to pick firstFirst page to open
Beginner, first EU application, small teamA cascade (FSTP) call: short form, no PIC needed in many casesPortal Calls for proposals with the cascade filter
Startup or SME that needs €50k–€200k quicklyCascade calls in your sector, sorted by deadlineSame Portal filter, then each project's call page
Consultant or grants office checking calls every dayA saved Portal search URL plus the Portal RSS feedSearch funding opportunities manual
Researcher who wants a personal grantERC or MSCA (direct grants, not cascade)ERC Starting Grant page
Region, city or NGO working on climate adaptationMission Adaptation cascade projects, then LIFEEU Mission: Adaptation to Climate Change
Tight budget, can't co-fund muchHorizon Europe cascade calls (often lump sums), not Digital Europe cascades with 50% co-fundingNCP Flanders FSTP infosheet

Why these picks: cascade calls are smaller and simpler, which suits beginners and small budgets. A saved search saves time for anyone checking calls every day. ERC and MSCA follow fixed annual dates, so researchers should plan around those dates and not around cascade rounds.

What Is Cascade Funding and How Does It Differ from Direct EU Grants?

Cascade funding (Financial Support to Third Parties, FSTP) is sub-granting. An EU-funded consortium passes part of its budget to outside organisations through simplified open calls, so you never go through the full Horizon Europe process yourself (BAYFOR).

Here is how the money moves. The Commission funds a project, say a digital innovation hub network or a climate adaptation programme. The grant agreement already includes a budget line for "financial support to third parties". The consortium writes its own call, publishes it, evaluates the applications and signs small agreements with the winners. You deal with the consortium. You don't deal with the Commission.

The official limits

The Horizon Europe rules set a default ceiling. According to the Annotated Grant Agreement (AGA), each recipient can get at most €60,000, unless the action's objective "would otherwise be impossible or overly difficult" to reach. In that case a higher amount must be set out in the call. NCP Flanders notes that higher amounts "appear regularly on the portal". It also notes that Digital Europe cascade grants usually pay 50% of eligible costs, so the recipient covers the other 50%.

Cascade / FSTP sub-grantDirect Horizon Europe grant
Who you apply toThe project consortiumThe Commission or its executive agency
Where the call is publishedPortal listing + project websitePortal topic page
Typical size€50,000–€200,000 (BAYFOR)Often several million euros per consortium
Typical duration6–18 months (same source)2–5 years
PIC needed?Often not (NCP Flanders)Yes
Consortium needed?Usually single applicant or small teamUsually 3+ partners
Form of paymentLump sum, prize or actual costs (varies)Per grant agreement

For example, Pathways2Resilience is a Mission Adaptation project. In its second call it selected 61 regional sub-grantees, and each received €210,000 for 18 months (January 2026–June 2027). That is well above the €60,000 default, which the AGA's exception allows.

If you later want a direct grant, you will need a PIC. Our guide to EU Funding and Tenders Portal registration: PIC in 6 steps covers that.

Where Do I Find the Live List of Open Cascade Funding Calls on the Portal?

The live list is on the Portal's Calls for proposals search page, filtered by Type of grants calls → "Calls for funding in cascade (issued by funded projects)". Many projects also advertise on their own websites, and no single directory covers everything (NCP Flanders).

Consortia are required to publish their cascade calls on the Portal, under the Horizon Europe General Annexes and Digital Europe call documents (same source). The publishing process explains why the list can lag a little. The project coordinator drafts the call and submits it. The Commission Project Officer gets a notification, previews the call and clicks Publish. Only then does the status change from "Submitted" to "Published" and the call appear in search (EC IT How To).

Steps to reach the list

  1. Go to the EU Funding & Tenders Portal and open Search funding & tenders → Calls for proposals.
  2. Open All filters (on some screen sizes the filter panel is on the left).
  3. Under Type of grants calls, tick Calls for funding in cascade (issued by funded projects) (EC IT How To).
  4. Under Status, keep only Open for submission and Forthcoming, so closed calls drop out (BAYFOR recommends removing closed calls).
  5. If you only want research-type calls, set Programme to Horizon Europe. Leave it blank to include Digital Europe cascades as well.
  6. Open a result. The Portal entry gives you the title, the dates and a link to the project's own call page. Follow that link for the guide for applicants.
  7. Copy the browser URL. The Portal stores your filters in the address bar (for example status=31094502 for open calls), so the bookmark reloads the same search.

Common mistakes and fixes

  • Searching keywords only. If you type "cascade" into the main search box, you will miss calls that don't use the word. Use the Type of grants calls filter instead.
  • Reading only the Portal entry. The Portal listing is a summary. Eligibility, the maximum grant and the evaluation criteria are in the project's guide for applicants, so always download it.
  • Missing project-only promotion. Some consortia announce a call on their website or LinkedIn days before the Officer publishes it on the Portal. Once you've found projects in your field, bookmark their "Open call" pages.
  • No updates between visits. The Portal offers a "Funding Opportunities RSS feed" (Online Manual). Add it to any RSS reader to see new items without running the search again.

How Do I Filter Open Calls by Deadline and Ticket Size?

Filter the Portal by status, programme and dates, then sort by deadline. You can't filter ticket size on the Portal, so you need a short manual pass through each project's call page.

The Portal's call search offers Status, Type of grants calls, Programme, date filters and a Sort control (Portal Calls for proposals). Grant amount isn't a filter field. The amount is set separately by each consortium, and the AGA only fixes the €60,000 default ceiling (AGA).

A workable routine (about 20 minutes a week)

  1. Run your saved cascade search (status Open + Forthcoming).
  2. In Sort, choose to sort by deadline, so the calls closing soonest come first.
  3. Drop anything closing within 10 days unless you already have a draft ready.
  4. Open the remaining calls one by one and record the facts below in a simple spreadsheet.
  5. Order the spreadsheet by "max per applicant", then by deadline.
Column to recordWhere to find itWhy it matters
Deadline + time zoneProject guide for applicantsMany close at 12:00 or 17:00 CET/CEST, not midnight
Max grant per applicantGuide, "Financial support" sectionNot on the Portal
Funding rateGuideDigital Europe cascades often pay 50% (NCP Flanders)
Form (lump sum / actual costs)GuideLump sums need less financial reporting
Eligible countries and entity typesGuide, "Eligibility"Varies per project
Submission platformProject siteOften a third-party form tool, not the Portal

For example, if two calls both close in six weeks, one paying up to €60,000 as a lump sum and the other €100,000 at a 50% rate, the second needs you to fund €100,000 of your own costs to receive the full amount. For a small company with little cash, the first call is often the better choice.

Pitfall: some calls list "total call budget" (say €3 million) very prominently. That figure is the total for all winners, not your ticket. Look for "per third party" or "per applicant".

For direct SME grants with fixed EU deadlines, see EU Funding for SMEs: 7 open 2026 calls and how to qualify.

Is Cascade Open Today? How to Check Current Status Quickly

There is no single call named "Cascade", so "is cascade open today" has no single answer. Each project runs its own calls, and you check that project's call page for its status and exact deadline.

People who search "is cascade open" usually saw the word in a newsletter or on a project page. The quickest check takes three steps:

  1. Find the project name. It will be an acronym (for example Pathways2Resilience). If you only know the topic, run the Portal cascade filter with a keyword.
  2. Open the project's "Open call" page. Look at the status label and the deadline, including the hour and time zone. That page is the authority. The Portal mirrors it.
  3. Check the project on CORDIS. Search the acronym on CORDIS. The project page shows the start and end dates. If the project ends in a few months, no new calls are coming. For example, the Pathways2Resilience CORDIS record (ID 101093942) shows the project details and the funding programme.

If the project site and the Portal disagree, trust the project's guide for applicants and email the call helpdesk listed in it. Portal entries depend on the Officer publishing updates (EC IT How To), so a corrected deadline can take time to show up there.

Is Cascade Still Open or Has It Closed? Tracking Call Timelines

Whether a cascade call is "still open" depends on the round. Projects often run several calls or cut-offs over their lifetime, so a closed round doesn't mean the project has stopped funding.

A cascade project typically opens one, two or more rounds. Pathways2Resilience is a clear example. It allocated €21 million across two funding cycles, and the second open call for regional authorities closed on 20 August 2025 at 12:00 CET (ERRIN; Climate-KIC). Its selected regions run from January 2026 to June 2027, so a region that missed August 2025 should not expect a third P2R round in that cycle.

Signal on the project pageWhat it usually meansWhat to do
"Call 2 closed", call 3 announcedAnother round is plannedNote the expected date and prepare now
"Final call" or the last numbered roundNo more funding from this projectLook for sister projects under the same topic
Project end date within 6–9 months (CORDIS)Too late for new sub-projectsSkip
Rolling call with cut-off datesApplications batched at each cut-offAim for the earliest cut-off with budget left

Common mistakes:

  • Relying on an old newsletter. Aggregator posts stay online long after a deadline. Always check the date on the project's own page.
  • Assuming the next round copies the last. Budgets, eligible countries and maximum amounts often change between rounds. Re-read the new guide.
  • Missing pre-registration. Some calls need an account on the submission platform days before the deadline. Register when the call opens.

What Open EU Funding Calls Exist for Climate Resilience in 2025-2026?

The main 2026 climate resilience deadlines for direct grants passed in September 2026. As of October 2026, what remains is cascade calls from Mission Adaptation projects and calls that open later in the 2026–2027 work programme cycle.

These are the official dates that shaped 2026:

CallTypeKey numbersDeadline (status as of 21 Oct 2026)
LIFE-2026-CLIMA-SAP-CCA Climate Change AdaptationDirect (LIFE)Indicative €28 million; part of the €601.5 million LIFE 2026 package (CINEA; Zabala)22 Sept 2026, 17:00 CEST, closed
HORIZON-MISS-2026-01 (Mission Adaptation, CLIMA-01 to -07)Direct (Horizon Europe)Topics range from National Adaptation Hubs to inland waterway resilience (Charles University overview)23 Sept 2026, closed
HORIZON-CL5-2026-07 (Climate science, e.g. D1-02 climate risk assessments)Direct (Horizon Europe)Opened 18 Dec 2025 (IUK Business Connect)16 Apr 2026, closed
Pathways2Resilience call 2Cascade€210,000 per region, 61 regions (Climate-KIC)20 Aug 2025, closed

The Cluster 5 work programme has calls closing as late as December 2027 (IUK Business Connect), so open the Cluster 5 and Missions work programme PDFs (Missions WP 2026-2027) and note the 2027 topics now.

To find climate cascade calls that are open today:

  1. Run the cascade filter on the Portal and type "climate", "adaptation" or "resilience" in the search box.
  2. Open the Mission Adaptation page. Mission projects that support regions often run sub-grant schemes.
  3. Check whether CORDIS shows an end date far enough ahead for a new round.

For example, a municipality that missed LIFE in September 2026 could apply for a cascade sub-grant now to build a local adaptation plan. That work makes a stronger LIFE or Mission application in the next cycle.

What ERC and MSCA Open Calls Are Available for Researchers in 2026?

ERC and MSCA have fixed annual deadlines, and they are direct grants, not cascade funding. As of 21 October 2026, the ERC Consolidator Grant 2027 call and the MSCA Doctoral Networks 2026 call are still open.

CallOpensDeadlineBudgetStatus on 21 Oct 2026
ERC Starting Grant 202722 Jul 202614 Oct 2026€594 million, ~373 grantsClosed
ERC Consolidator Grant 202724 Sep 202612 Jan 2027€618 millionOpen
ERC Proof of Concept 202712 Nov 202610 Mar 2027 and 16 Sep 2027€60 millionForthcoming
ERC Synergy Grant 202717 Feb 202711 May 2027€500 millionForthcoming
ERC Advanced Grant 202727 May 202726 Aug 2027€798 millionForthcoming
ERC Plus 20271 Jun 20271 Sep 2027€210 millionForthcoming
MSCA Postdoctoral Fellowships 20269 Apr 20269 Sep 2026€434 millionClosed
MSCA Doctoral Networks 202628 May 202624 Nov 2026€628 million, 130+ projects, 1,950 doctoral candidatesOpen

ERC dates and budgets come from the ERC Work Programme 2027 as summarised by Hezelburcht and UKRO. UKRO notes that the Synergy opening was moved to February 2027. MSCA figures come from the MSCA PF announcement and the Doctoral Networks announcement. The ERC Starting Grant awards up to €1.5 million over five years (ERC).

Eligibility changed for 2027. Starting Grant applicants qualify if they defended their PhD in the ten years before 1 January 2027, and Consolidator applicants five to fifteen years after the PhD. Researchers may hold at most one Starting and one Consolidator Grant in their career (Hezelburcht).

The distinction matters for your search. ERC and MSCA calls never appear under the cascade filter. Search them on the Portal by programme ("Horizon Europe") and call ID instead. If you are writing a collaborative Horizon proposal rather than an ERC one, our Horizon Europe Part B 2026 scoring map shows how evaluators read each section.

Next steps

You can do the core work yourself today in under an hour. If you'd prefer help, free official advisers are available.

DIY actions for today

  1. Build and bookmark the Portal search: Calls for proposals → Type of grants calls → Calls for funding in cascade (issued by funded projects) → Status: Open for submission + Forthcoming, sorted by deadline.
  2. Start the six-column spreadsheet from the filtering section and fill it for the first five calls that match your sector.
  3. If you are a researcher, put 24 November 2026 (MSCA DN) and 12 January 2027 (ERC CoG) in your calendar and check your eligibility window today.

If you'd rather not do it alone

  • National Contact Points (NCPs): free, government-funded advisers for Horizon Europe in each country. For example, NCP Flanders publishes FSTP guidance. NCPs suit first-time applicants who want rule checks. They aren't for you if you want someone to write the proposal, because NCPs advise but don't draft. Their capacity is also limited near big deadlines.
  • Regional innovation agencies and grants offices. University research offices and regional bodies such as BAYFOR in Bavaria give free advice to eligible organisations. The limitation is that they only serve their own region or institution.
  • Private grant consultants: paid, and fee models vary (day rates, fixed fees, success fees). Ask for a written quote and check current terms on the consultant's own page (as of October 2026). Consultants can make sense for an SME applying to several calls at once. For a single €60,000 lump-sum sub-grant, the fee may not be worth it.

Related guides on this site

  • EU Funding and Tenders Portal Registration: PIC in 6 Steps
  • EU Funding for SMEs: 7 Open 2026 Calls and How to Qualify
  • Horizon Europe Proposal Template Part B: 2026 Scoring Map

FAQ

Who is Cascade Capital Funding LLC?

It is a US company name with no link to EU cascade funding. One entity with this name is an Oregon non-profit SBA Certified Development Company that has supported local small businesses since 1983 (SEDCOR directory). A separate entity of the same name appears in California regulatory records (DFPI). Neither handles EU sub-grants.

What is the typical ticket size for a cascade/FSTP sub-grant?

Under Horizon Europe, the default ceiling is €60,000 per third party, and higher amounts are allowed when the call justifies them (AGA). In practice, BAYFOR reports typical ranges of €50,000–€200,000 (BAYFOR). Some calls go higher, like Pathways2Resilience's €210,000.

How many cut-off dates does a typical cascade call have?

There is no fixed number. Each consortium decides in its grant agreement, and many run two or more rounds over the project's life. Pathways2Resilience, for example, ran two funding cycles (ERRIN). Check the project page and its CORDIS end date to see whether more rounds are realistic.

Can non-EU organisations apply to cascade funding open calls?

Sometimes. Each call's guide for applicants defines the eligible countries and entity types, and the rules differ from project to project (BAYFOR). Read the "Eligibility" section before you start writing. If it's unclear, email the call helpdesk.
