item.title: EIC Accelerator Deadlines: 2026 Cut-Off Dates and Steps
item.dc:creator: Aoba Works
item.description: EIC Accelerator deadlines for 2026 explained: six full-proposal cut-offs, monthly short-application batches, draft 2027 dates, and the key steps to complete before the 4 November cut-off.
item.content:encoded:
How this guide was made: drafted with AI assistance from the official sources linked below, then passed an automated editorial check before publishing. Our process

The EIC Accelerator deadlines for 2026 are six full-proposal cut-offs: 7 January, 4 March, 6 May, 8 July, 2 September and 4 November 2026, each at 17:00 Brussels time (EIC Accelerator page). You can submit a short application at any time. Short applications are collected into a batch for evaluation on the first Tuesday of every month. As of 21 October 2026, the only cut-off left this year is 4 November, and you can only submit to it if your short application has already received a "GO".

Which option is right for you?

Choose your route based on where your application stands today. The table names the first page to open for each situation.

Your situationWhat to pick firstFirst page to open
New to EIC, no PIC yetRegister your organisation, then write the short applicationFunding & Tenders Portal + our PIC guide
You already have a short-application GOSubmit the full proposal by 4 November 2026, 17:00 BrusselsEIC Accelerator page
Short application not yet sentAim for the 3 November 2026 batch, then target an early-2027 cut-offCall HORIZON-EIC-2026-ACCELERATOR-01
Early-stage (TRL 4) start-up in a Widening countryWatch for the next EIC Pre-Accelerator call insteadCORDIS call record
Small budget, no consultantFree help from your National Contact Point or Enterprise Europe NetworkEEN
Your technology may fit a strategic topicCompare the Challenges with the Open call before you writeEIC Work Programme 2026 PDF

If you're still deciding whether the EIC suits you at all, our overview of EU funding for SMEs: 7 open 2026 calls compares it with less competitive options.

What Are the EIC Accelerator Deadlines for 2026?

The 2026 EIC Accelerator has six fixed full-proposal cut-offs and a short application that stays open all year. The EIC moved to a schedule of one cut-off every two months for 2026. This replaced the two cut-offs it ran in 2025.

These dates come from the official EIC Accelerator page and the Cyprus national funding portal's summary of call HORIZON-EIC-2026-ACCELERATOR-01. Status is as of October 2026:

Full-proposal cut-off (17:00 Brussels)Status on 21 Oct 2026
7 January 2026Closed
4 March 2026Closed
6 May 2026Closed
8 July 2026Closed
2 September 2026Closed
4 November 2026Open, and the last cut-off of 2026

According to the Cyprus portal, if your short application succeeds under the 2026 Work Programme, you can send your full proposal to any of these 2026 dates. The call opened on 6 November 2025. Its budget is €634 million: €414 million for EIC Accelerator Open and €220 million for EIC Accelerator Challenges (Cyprus portal).

Pitfalls with the 2026 dates

  • Third-party sites show different "deadline" dates. Aggregators list different closing dates for the same call ID. One shows 17 December, another shows 4 November (euacc.ai, Cyprus portal). To fix this, trust only the deadline shown on the official topic page and the batching dates in the Work Programme PDF.
  • Time zone. The 17:00 cut-off is Brussels time (CET/CEST). For example, a team in Lisbon or Dublin has until 16:00 local time. A team in Helsinki has until 18:00.
  • Interviews follow every second cut-off, not every one. Jury interview sessions are organised after every second full-proposal batch, and tentative dates are posted on the EIC website (Cyprus portal). Keep that period free in the team's calendar.

What Are the EIC Accelerator Deadlines for 2027?

The 2027 EIC Accelerator dates are only in draft: 3 February, 1 April, 1 September and 3 November 2027. A draft of the EIC Work Programme 2027 dated 7 July 2026 lists these four full-proposal cut-offs. That draft is labelled as not adopted or endorsed by the European Commission (evolution-europe summary of the draft). As of October 2026, no adopted 2027 programme turned up in the sources checked. So treat these dates as planning estimates, not commitments.

Draft 2027 cut-offGap since the previous cut-off
3 February 20273 months after 4 Nov 2026
1 April 20272 months
1 September 20275 months
3 November 20272 months

The draft makes three changes that affect planning (evolution-europe, Myriad Associates, 24 Aug 2026):

  1. The number of cut-offs falls from six to four. Missing April 2027 would mean waiting five months for the next one.
  2. A new "GO Reserve" list lets the jury hold strong near-misses. They could be funded if budget is left over after the year's selections (Rasph summary).
  3. Challenge topics fall from five to four. The draft sets €150 million across climate-neutral and smart cities (€50m), carbon removal and circularity (€50m), in-situ ocean observation (€30m) and fusion power plants (€20m).

Pitfall: don't make investor or hiring commitments that depend on the draft dates. Fix: plan for an April 2027 submission and keep September 2027 as the fallback. Recheck once the Commission announces adoption. The 2026 programme's adoption was announced on the Commission press corner, so watch there.

What Were the EIC Accelerator Deadlines for 2025?

The 2025 EIC Accelerator had only two full-proposal cut-offs: 12 March 2025 and 1 October 2025. Short applications were batched on the first Tuesday of each month, as they are now (ERRIN call listing, Segler Consulting). Both dates are closed, and a 2025 GO does not entitle you to submit under 2026 rules automatically. Check the eligibility section of the 2026 Work Programme before you rely on an older result.

YearFull-proposal cut-offsCountShort-application batching
202512 Mar, 1 Oct2First Tuesday monthly
20267 Jan, 4 Mar, 6 May, 8 Jul, 2 Sep, 4 Nov6First Tuesday monthly
2027 (draft)3 Feb, 1 Apr, 1 Sep, 3 Nov4First Tuesday monthly

Across these three years, the number of cut-offs changes but the short-application rhythm does not. So plan your preparation around the monthly batch, then pick a cut-off.

What Are the Current EIC Accelerator Submission Dates?

The current schedule has a monthly short-application batch and one remaining full-proposal cut-off on 4 November 2026. Short proposals are "batched for evaluation every first Tuesday of the month at 5pm Brussels time" (EIC).

Here are the dates that matter from today, 21 October 2026:

DateWhat happensSource
3 Nov 2026 (Tue), 17:00Next short-application batch (first Tuesday of November)EIC
4 Nov 2026, 17:00Last 2026 full-proposal cut-offEIC
1 Dec 2026 (Tue), 17:00December short-application batchSame monthly rule
3 Feb 2027, 17:00First draft 2027 full-proposal cut-offDraft WP 2027 summary

Each stage takes roughly this long, according to the official EIC page:

StageWhat you submitTypical result time
1. Short proposal12-page form, pitch deck of up to 10 slides (PDF), video of up to 3 minutes4–6 weeks
2. Full proposal20-page form, pitch deck, implementation plan, financial information, Letters of Intent, FTO analysis, 3-minute video8–9 weeks
3. Jury interviewLive pitch to the EIC Jury2–3 weeks after interview week
4. Due diligence (equity component)Investment documentation2–6 months to an investment decision

For example, say a short application goes into the 3 November batch and gets results after four to six weeks. That means early-to-mid December 2026. By then the last 2026 cut-off has passed, so the realistic full-proposal target becomes the first 2027 cut-off. Whether a GO received in late 2026 can be used for a 2027 cut-off depends on the transition rules in the adopted 2027 programme. Confirm this with your National Contact Point rather than assuming it.

How Does EIC Accelerator Submission Deadlines Work (Step-by-Step)?

You can submit a short application at any time. A GO lets you submit a full proposal by a fixed cut-off, and that is followed by remote evaluation and then a jury interview. Every proposal goes through the Funding & Tenders Portal, so start with your organisation's registration.

Steps from zero to full proposal

  1. Get a PIC. On the Funding & Tenders Portal, log in with your EU Login and register your organisation to receive a 9-digit Participant Identification Code. Our PIC registration guide walks through all six screens. If you're a natural person who hasn't founded the company yet, you can still apply (EIC).
  2. Open the topic. In the Portal, go to Search Funding & Tenders, search for HORIZON-EIC-2026-ACCELERATOR-01, and open the topic page.
  3. Pick Open or Challenge. Read the Challenge topics in the 2026 Work Programme. If your innovation fits one, the Challenges budget (€220m) is competing for a narrower field than Open (€414m).
  4. Start the short proposal. On the topic page, use Start submission, enter your PIC, and complete the 12-page short form. Upload a pitch deck of up to 10 slides as a PDF, and a video pitch of up to 3 minutes.
  5. Submit before the first Tuesday of the month, 17:00 Brussels. That puts your proposal in the month's batch. Expect a GO or NO-GO within 4–6 weeks.
  6. After a GO, build the full proposal. You need the 20-page form, an updated pitch deck, the implementation plan, financial information, customer or partner Letters of Intent, a freedom-to-operate (FTO) analysis and a new 3-minute video (EIC).
  7. Submit to a cut-off. Choose one of the batching dates and submit before 17:00 Brussels. The proposal is reviewed remotely by EIC experts, with results in 8–9 weeks.
  8. Prepare for the interview. If you're shortlisted, you pitch to the EIC Jury. Results arrive 2–3 weeks after the interview week.

Use the Horizon Europe Part B scoring map for general guidance on writing to the evaluation criteria. Keep in mind that the EIC uses its own templates and does not use the standard Part B.

Common mistakes and fixes

MistakeWhy it hurtsFix
Submitting a second application while the first is under evaluationOnly one application is allowed at a time (EIC)Wait for the result before resubmitting
Starting Letters of Intent and FTO analysis after the GOThese take outside parties weeks to deliverAsk for LoIs and commission the FTO while the short application is being evaluated
Uploading at 16:55 Brussels timePortal slowdowns can push you past the cut-offSubmit at least one working day early
Choosing a Challenge that only loosely fitsFit with the Challenge is part of the assessmentIf the fit is weak, use Open
Ignoring TRLThe Accelerator expects at least TRL 5 completed, and the grant funds TRL 6–8 work (euacc.ai, EIC)Earlier-stage teams should look at EIC Transition or Pre-Accelerator

What Is the EIC Pre-Accelerator and Its Deadline?

The EIC Pre-Accelerator is a separate, earlier-stage grant for deep-tech start-ups in Horizon Europe Widening countries. It has no 2026 call, and a 2027 call is expected. It is run jointly by the EIC and the Horizon Europe WIDERA programme. Its only deadline so far was 18 November 2025 (CORDIS: HORIZON-WIDERA-2025-02-ACCESS-01, Opportunity Desk). It is a Funding & Tenders Portal call, not an Enterprise Europe Network bootcamp. People often confuse it with national "pre-accelerator" programmes.

EIC Pre-Accelerator (2025 pilot)EIC Accelerator (2026)
WhoSingle SMEs in Widening countriesSMEs, start-ups, small mid-caps (up to 499 staff) in EU/Associated countries
Tech readinessAt least TRL 4At least TRL 5 completed
Grant€300k–€500k lump sum, 70% of costsUp to €2.5m, 70% of eligible costs
Budget€20m€634m
Deadline18 Nov 2025 (closed)Cut-offs every 2 months in 2026

Sources: Opportunity Desk, EIC, Cyprus portal.

On the 2026 gap, Catalyze states that "there is no Pre-Accelerator in 2026, but it is expected to return in 2027". It lists an indicative 2027 window of 5 May to 18 November 2027, €500k–€1m per project and a €40m budget (Catalyze). The draft EIC 2027 Work Programme itself contains no Pre-Accelerator section (evolution-europe). The call sits under WIDERA, so watch the WIDERA work programme, not the EIC one.

Pitfall: applying to the Accelerator at TRL 4 because the Pre-Accelerator is closed. Fix: use the time to reach TRL 5 and gather customer evidence. If you're in a Widening country, prepare for the expected 2027 Pre-Accelerator call.

How Much Is the EIC Accelerator Grant and When Is It Due?

The 2026 EIC Accelerator grant is up to €2.5 million, and investment of €1–10 million is available on top. You apply for both through the same short application and full-proposal cut-offs. The grant is a lump sum for TRL 6–8 activities completed within 24 months (EIC).

RouteWhat you get (2026)Note
Grant onlyUp to €2.5m, 70% of eligible costsListed for start-ups/SMEs (Cyprus portal)
Blended financeGrant (70% of costs) + €1–10m investmentThe investment needs due diligence of 2–6 months
Investment only€1–10m equity or quasi-equityLarger rounds are possible through STEP Scale-Up (EIC)

If a guide you're reading quotes a different equity ceiling, check its date against the official page. For 2026, the official range is €1–10 million per company in the Accelerator itself (as of October 2026, EIC). Larger amounts go through STEP Scale-Up, which is a separate call. One consultancy reports that a separate EIC STEP Defence Scale Up call offers up to €30 million and closes on 28 October 2026 (One Synergy). Check that call's own topic page before relying on it.

Payment timing: the grant is not paid at the cut-off. The steps are evaluation (8–9 weeks), the interview (results in 2–3 weeks), grant preparation and then the first payment, so plan cash flow accordingly. Applicants who pass the thresholds but aren't funded receive a Seal of Excellence, which some national programmes accept (EIC).

For example, a €3m project budget under grant-only would receive at most €2.1m (70%). The company would have to fund €0.9m itself. Show where that 30% comes from in the financial information.

Is the EIC Accelerator Open Right Now?

Yes, the EIC Accelerator is open: short applications are accepted at any time, and the 4 November 2026 full-proposal cut-off is still ahead. Only teams that already hold a GO can use the November cut-off.

To check the live status yourself:

  1. Open the topic page for HORIZON-EIC-2026-ACCELERATOR-01.
  2. Look at the Topic status label (Open / Forthcoming / Closed) and the deadline field in the General information box.
  3. Compare with the batching dates on the EIC Accelerator page.
  4. Once November passes, search the Portal for HORIZON-EIC-2027-ACCELERATOR. Aggregators already mention a 2027 call ID (euacc.ai), but only an official topic page confirms that it exists.

If you use the Portal's search filters, the same filter tips from our cascade funding guide apply, especially filtering by Open for submission.

Next steps

Today, choose your target cut-off and plan backwards from it.

Do-it-yourself actions for today

  1. Check that your organisation has a validated PIC. If it doesn't, follow the PIC registration guide today, because validation can take time.
  2. If you have no GO yet, draft the 12-page short form, the 10-slide deck and the 3-minute video. Aim for the 3 November 2026 batch at 17:00 Brussels, or 1 December if that's too tight.
  3. Download the 2026 Work Programme PDF and read the Challenge annexes to decide between Open and Challenge.

If you'd rather not do it alone

  • National Contact Points (NCPs): free, government-funded advisers for Horizon Europe in each EU and Associated country. They're a good fit if you want rule checks and a proposal pre-read. They don't fit if you need someone to write the proposal for you, because they won't. Capacity varies by country.
  • Enterprise Europe Network (EEN): free support for SMEs (as of October 2026; check the official page). EEN is useful for partner search and local guidance. It is not a dedicated proposal-writing service.
  • Private EIC consultancies: before you sign, ask each provider for its full fee structure, including any success fee, and what happens after a NO-GO, and get it in writing. A consultancy suits teams with funding but no writing time. It doesn't suit first-time applicants who haven't validated their own market story yet, and no consultant can guarantee a GO.

Related guides on this site

  • EU Funding for SMEs: 7 Open 2026 Calls and How to Qualify
  • Horizon Europe Proposal Template Part B: 2026 Scoring Map
  • Cascade Funding Open Calls: Portal Filters and 2026 Dates

FAQ

What is the EIC Accelerator open deadline?

There is no single closing date for short applications. They are open all year and batched on the first Tuesday of each month at 17:00 Brussels time (EIC). Full proposals have fixed cut-offs, and the last one in 2026 is 4 November.

What are the EIC Accelerator dates for 2026?

The full-proposal cut-offs are 7 January, 4 March, 6 May, 8 July, 2 September and 4 November 2026, all at 17:00 Brussels time. Interview sessions follow every second batch (Cyprus portal).

What are the EIC Accelerator deadlines for 2027?

A draft 2027 Work Programme lists 3 February, 1 April, 1 September and 3 November 2027. The draft has not been adopted, so the dates could change (evolution-europe). Check the Funding & Tenders Portal once the 2027 call is published.

Is there an EIC Pre-Accelerator deadline in 2026?

No. The pilot call closed on 18 November 2025, and sources say a new call is expected in 2027 (CORDIS, Catalyze). It is limited to start-ups in Widening countries at TRL 4 or higher.

item.title: EU Funding and Tenders Portal Registration: PIC in 6 Steps
item.dc:creator: Aoba Works
item.description: EU Funding and Tenders Portal registration in 6 wizard steps: EU Login, PIC, validation documents, LEAR appointment and fixes for VAT errors.
item.content:encoded:
How this guide was made: drafted with AI assistance from the official sources linked below, then passed an automated editorial check before publishing. Our process

EU Funding and Tenders Portal registration has two parts. First you create a personal EU Login account. Then you register your organisation in the Participant Register through a 6-step wizard, and that wizard gives you a 9-digit PIC (Participant Identification Code) straight away. Legal validation and the LEAR appointment usually come later, once a proposal you are part of has been selected, so a new PIC is enough to join and submit a proposal (Online Manual; IT How To: Registration steps).

Which option is right for you?

Start by checking whether your organisation already has a PIC. Registering a second one is the most common avoidable mistake, and most universities and many established companies are already in the register.

Your situationWhat to pick firstFirst page to open
Beginner: you have never used any EU systemCreate an EU Login, then search for an existing PICEU Login
Researcher at a university or large instituteAsk your research office for the existing PIC. Don't register a new oneParticipant Register search
Startup or SME applying for the first timeRun the 6-step wizard yourself. It's free and gives you a PIC on the spotRegister an organisation (IT How To)
Sole trader or freelancerRegister as a natural person and have your VAT or tax-exemption proof readyRules on Legal Entity Validation
Daily use: grant manager or consultant handling many PICsAsk each client's self-registrant to add you as an authorised user rather than sharing loginsRegistration steps (step 4)
Zero budget, need human helpYour National Contact Point or Enterprise Europe Network office, both freeEnterprise Europe Network on the Portal
You were just told your proposal is selectedGet validation documents and the LEAR letter ready nowLEAR appointment and validation

The reasons, one line each. Beginners need EU Login before anything else works. Institutions almost always have a PIC already. SMEs lose nothing by registering themselves. Sole traders follow a separate document path as natural persons. Consultants need their own access rights. Selected applicants have a validation clock running.

How to Register on the EU Funding and Tenders Portal (Step-by-Step)

There are two layers. An EU Login personal account comes first, then a separate organisation registration that creates your PIC, and you need both before you can submit a proposal. You can browse calls and read call documents on the Portal without logging in. The registration only matters when you want to join or submit a proposal.

Part A: Create your EU Login

  1. Go to the EU Login page and click Create an account.
  2. Enter your First name, Last name and E-mail, confirm the email and choose your E-mail language.
  3. Type the on-screen verification code, accept the privacy statement and click Create an account (EURES guide to EU Login).
  4. Open the activation email and set your password from the link.
  5. Set up two-factor authentication. The Portal's IT guide says 2FA on EU Login became mandatory over the course of 2026. Register a method (the EU Login Mobile App, a security key, a passkey or eID), enable it in your security settings and answer three security questions. The guide recommends registering more than one method so you don't get locked out.

Use a work email address, not a personal one. The account is yours personally, but organisation roles get attached to it.

Part B: Register the organisation and get the PIC

  1. Open the Participant Register page and search for your organisation first.
  2. If nothing comes up, sign in and click Register your organisation (IT How To).
  3. Go through the six wizard steps: identification details, organisation data, legal information, authorised users, summary and success. Each step is covered in the section on registering an organisation below.
  4. Copy the PIC from the success screen into your proposal team's shared notes.

Once you finish, the organisation shows up under My Organisations with the status Declared, meaning not yet validated. Your EU Login gets the Self-registrant role (IT How To).

For example, a two-person software startup could create EU Logins on Monday morning, register the company before lunch and give the PIC to a consortium coordinator the same day. Nobody at the Commission has to approve anything at that point.

EU Funding and Tenders Portal Sign Up: EU Login vs Organization Registration

EU Login is your personal identity, an email and password you use across EU systems. Organisation registration in the Participant Register happens once per legal entity and issues the PIC. People often mix the two up. "Signing up" to the Portal means creating an EU Login, and that alone doesn't make your organisation a participant.

EU LoginOrganisation registration (PIC)
What it identifiesA personA legal entity (or a natural person acting as one)
How manyOne per personOne per legal entity. Duplicates get merged or blocked
Wherewebgate.ec.europa.eu/casParticipant Register
OutputLogin credentials and a 2FA method9-digit PIC, status "Declared"
Needed forLogging in, joining a proposal as a contactBeing listed as a participant in a proposal
Who checks itNobody. It's self-serviceThe Central Validation Service, later (Online Manual)
If the person leavesThe account leaves with themThe PIC stays with the organisation

Common pitfalls:

  • Registering the organisation under one person's private account. If that person leaves before validation, nobody else can update the record. Fix: add a backup authorised user in wizard step 4 (Registration steps).
  • Treating the PIC as a personal ID. A researcher who moves universities doesn't take the PIC along. They use the new institution's PIC.
  • Several colleagues each registering "just in case". The wizard flags possible duplicates by legal name and country, but similar spellings can still get past it. Agree internally on who registers.

How to Register an Organization in the EU Funding & Tenders Portal

You enter the legal name, VAT or registration number, address, language and legal form, then name the authorised users. Supporting documents are uploaded later, when the Central Validation Service asks for them. The wizard marks mandatory fields with a red asterisk, shows errors in red, and has a Save button so you can keep a draft and come back to it (IT How To: Participant register).

The six wizard steps and their labels

Based on the official Registration steps page (as of October 2026):

  1. Organisation identification. Enter the Legal name and VAT number. For EU countries the wizard checks the VAT number against national databases and shows a warning icon if it can't find it. It also lists "possible duplicates based on the provided Legal name and registration country". If one of them is yours, click Use this PIC to contact that organisation's current LEAR instead of carrying on.
  2. Organisation data. Main contact details, legal address and the organisation's official language. If the address doesn't match the VAT register, a message tells you. For Spain and Germany the check covers only the VAT number.
  3. Legal information. Pick the Legal form from the dropdown and fill in the extra legal data it asks for, such as registration authority, registration date and registration number.
  4. Authorised users. Your EU Login is added automatically. You can add a backup user with self-registrant rights, who can update data or upload documents after registration.
  5. Summary. Every field is shown with Edit buttons. Read the legal name one letter at a time here.
  6. Success. Your new PIC appears, and you can use it in a proposal immediately.

What to have open before you start

For validation, the Commission compares your data with official documents. The REA Central Validation Service lists a legal entity form (dated, stamped and signed), a VAT extract less than 1 year old (or proof of VAT exemption), a registration extract less than 1 year old for private bodies, the law or decree for public bodies, and statutes for non-profits (REA Central Validation Service presentation). You don't upload these in the wizard. Having them open while you type, though, keeps what you register identical to what you'll later prove.

Example: if your trade register extract says "Nordlicht Analytics GmbH" and your website says "Nordlicht", type Nordlicht Analytics GmbH in Legal name. The short brand name goes in the business name field, if you use one.

Pitfalls and fixes

  • VAT warning icon in step 1. Check the format first (country prefix, no spaces). If your national VIES record is out of date, fix it with your tax office. Don't type a different number to make the warning go away.
  • Address mismatch message in step 2. Use the registered legal seat, not your office or co-working address.
  • Wrong legal form. A foundation registered as a company, or a public university registered as a private body, causes problems at validation because the status (public/private, for-profit/non-profit) is checked against your statutes (Rules on LEV, LEAR and FCA).

If you are about to use the PIC in a Horizon Europe proposal, the participant table in Part A of the form pulls data from this register. Our Horizon Europe Part B scoring map covers the narrative half of that same submission.

What Is a PIC Number and How Long Does It Take to Get One

A PIC (Participant Identification Code) is a 9-digit ID that the wizard issues instantly when you submit it. Legal validation is a separate, later step, and for grants it is triggered only after a proposal you're in has been evaluated successfully (Online Manual).

So there are two different timelines:

StageWhen it happensTypical trigger
PIC issuedRight away, on the wizard's success screenYou finish the 6 steps (Registration steps)
Status "Declared"From registration until validatedDefault for new records
Validation requestAfter the evaluation result letterYour proposal is selected for funding
LEAR appointmentAfter the organisation is validatedNotification sent to the self-registrant (LEAR page)

How long validation takes depends on how fast you send correct documents and whether the Central Validation Service needs to ask more questions. The official pages don't give one fixed number of days. The deadline that applies to you is in the request message, so read it the day it arrives.

Not everyone needs validation. It applies to beneficiaries and affiliated entities in grants and to contractors in procurement, but not to associated partners or subcontractors (Online Manual).

Example: an NGO that joins a consortium as an associated partner gets a PIC, appears in the proposal, and may never go through full legal validation for that project.

Why Was My EU Portal Registration Rejected? Common Validation Errors

Most problems come from four things: a VAT number that doesn't match national records, a legal name or address that differs from your official documents, documents that are expired or the wrong type, and LEAR paperwork signed by someone who can't prove their authority. The wizard almost never "rejects" you. What stalls is validation, when the Central Validation Service compares your registered data with your documents. And all messages go through the Participant Register only, never by email (Online Manual).

ProblemWhat it looks likeFix
VAT mismatchWarning icon in wizard step 1, or a validation request for a VAT documentUpload a VAT extract less than 1 year old. If you aren't VAT-registered, upload proof of exemption (REA CVS)
Trading name used as legal nameName on the extract differs from the registerRequest a correction so Legal name matches the extract exactly
Old registration extractExtract older than 1 yearGet a fresh extract from your national business register
Wrong entity typeSole trader registered as a companyRe-check the natural-person rules (next sections) and ask for a correction
LEAR letter not acceptedMissing signature, unclear authority, no ID copiesRe-sign in blue ink or with a qualified e-signature, and add an ID copy and proof of the signatory's authority (LEAR page)
Duplicate PICValidation asks which record is the real oneKeep the PIC used in proposals and ask for the other one to be merged or deactivated
Request ignoredNo reply by the deadlineAnswer in the Participant Register, not by email

How to reply to a validation request:

  1. Sign in, open My Organisations and find the organisation.
  2. Open the message or document request from the Central Validation Service.
  3. Upload exactly the document type asked for, in a legible scan.
  4. If data needs to change too, edit it and click Submit changes. Changed fields show a pencil icon until they're validated (IT How To).

Example: a small Portuguese company that registered its office street instead of its registered seat would upload the current certidão permanente and correct the address in the same reply. That's one round instead of two.

If you're using an IT problem as an excuse to miss a deadline, don't. Contact the Portal IT helpdesk and keep the ticket number.

How to Appoint a LEAR (Legal Entity Appointed Representative) After Registration

Your organisation's legal representative appoints the LEAR with a signed appointment letter that you upload to the Participant Register. The Central Validation Service has to validate the appointment before your organisation can sign grant agreements electronically. Without a LEAR, "it will NOT be possible to update the legal entity data in the Participant Register, nor sign any contracts electronically in the Portal" (LEAR appointment and validation).

The LEAR is the person formally responsible for everything your organisation does in the Portal. The LEAR can also appoint Legal Signatories and Financial Signatories and manage access rights.

Steps, using the official menu labels

  1. Wait for the trigger. The self-registrant gets a notification from the Central Validation Service asking them to start the LEAR procedure. Organisation validation has to come first.
  2. Choose two people. You need the LEAR candidate and a legal representative with authority under your statutes, typically a CEO, rector or director-general.
  3. Enter the data. Go to My Organisations > Actions > View organisation details > Authorised users/Lear section > Add Lear and enter names and contact details for both people.
  4. Generate the letter. The system produces the LEAR appointment letter (the official template includes the LEAR roles and duties). It also checks whether the LEAR already has an EU Login.
  5. Sign. The legal representative and the LEAR both date and sign, either in blue ink or with a qualified electronic signature under eIDAS.
  6. Upload. Upload the signed letter, ID or passport copies for both signatories, and a document that names the legal representative and shows their power to act.
  7. Activate. After validation, the LEAR gets activation instructions by email and can get a PIN by SMS.

Pitfalls and fixes

  • A simple scanned signature or a non-qualified e-signature. Only blue ink or a qualified e-signature is accepted. Re-sign.
  • Proof of authority that doesn't name the person. A generic board resolution isn't enough. The document has to name the legal representative and their role.
  • Joint representation. If your statutes need two directors to sign together, both have to sign.
  • Picking someone who's about to leave. Choose a stable role such as a research office head or finance manager, and plan backups through Account Administrator appointments (Online Manual roles).

The organisation has to keep the original signed documents for as long as it uses the Portal and through the EU control retention periods (LEAR page).

EU Funding and Tenders Portal Registration for Individuals, Startups, and NGOs: Does It Differ?

Every entity type goes through the same wizard. What changes is the legal form, the status you declare, and the documents that validation asks for. The biggest split is between natural persons and legal persons.

The validation rules say that self-employed people, such as craftspeople, liberal professions or traders, count as natural persons, not private bodies. Their business doesn't have a legal personality separate from them. A natural person needs an official VAT document, or proof of VAT exemption, not older than 6 months, plus a legible copy of a valid ID card or passport. For natural persons, the participant is automatically the LEAR and the role can't go to anyone else (Rules on LEV, LEAR and FCA).

EntityHow to registerValidation documents (if requested)Watch out for
Sole trader / freelancerAs a natural person. Enter your VAT number if you have oneVAT document or exemption proof less than 6 months old, plus ID copyYou're your own LEAR. No proof of capacity is needed, but you still enter the LEAR data
Startup / SME (company)Legal person, private, for-profitLegal entity form, VAT extract and registration extract, each less than 1 year old (REA CVS)SME status is assessed separately from legal validation
NGO / association / foundationLegal person, private, non-profitStatutes plus legal entity form and VAT or exemption proofDeclare non-profit status only if your statutes support it
Public university / public bodyLegal person, publicLaw, decree or decision establishing the bodyIt usually already has a PIC. Search first
Non-EU organisationSame wizard. The VAT database check covers EU countriesNational registration and tax documentsTranslations may be requested

Example: a freelance translator in Belgium with a VAT number registers as a natural person and enters that VAT number. A two-founder BV in the Netherlands registers as a private, for-profit legal person. Both get a PIC in the same 6 steps.

If you're a startup still choosing which calls to target, our overview of open 2026 EU calls for SMEs explains eligibility before you spend time on registration.

How to Find and Edit Your Organization's PIC After Registration

You find an existing PIC with the search on the Participant Register page. You edit it from My Organisations: the self-registrant can do that while the record is unvalidated, and only the LEAR or an Account Administrator can request changes once it's validated (Online Manual).

Find a PIC

  1. Open the Participant Register page.
  2. Search by organisation name (try the legal name and the short name) and narrow by country.
  3. If you're still not sure, ask your finance or research office. Large organisations sometimes hold more than one historical record.
  4. If the PIC belongs to your organisation but you have no access, use the contact option shown for that record, or Use this PIC in the wizard, to reach the current LEAR (Registration steps).

Edit organisation data

  1. Sign in and open My Organisations.
  2. Next to the organisation, open Actions and choose View organisation details (older guides call it Modify organisation).
  3. Use the left menu to find the data group, such as address or legal data.
  4. Change the fields. A yellow or red pencil marks unsubmitted or unvalidated changes, and a green tick marks validated data.
  5. Click Submit changes. For a validated entity, upload a supporting document for legal changes such as a new name or seat (IT How To).

Common mistake: registering a new PIC because the old one has an outdated address. Update the existing record instead. A new PIC means another duplicate to sort out later.

Next steps

You can do the free part today, and the paid options are only worth it if your time is worth more than the fee.

What to do today

  1. Create your EU Login and register two 2FA methods (2FA guide).
  2. Search the Participant Register for your organisation. If it isn't there, gather your trade register extract and VAT document, then run the 6-step wizard.
  3. Put a short note in your shared files with the PIC, the self-registrant's name, the backup user, and who could become LEAR.

If you'd rather not do it yourself

  • National Contact Points (free). Every Horizon Europe country has NCPs that give free, confidential advice on administrative questions like this (Ideal-ist: What is an NCP; example: FFG Austria). They suit researchers and first-time applicants. They're less useful if you want someone to do the clicking for you, because NCPs advise rather than register on your behalf.
  • Enterprise Europe Network (free for SMEs). EEN offices help SMEs with access to EU funding and partner search (EEN on the Portal; EEN access to EU funding). They fit startups and SMEs. Universities and large firms usually have in-house support instead. Capacity differs between regional offices.
  • Private grant consultants (paid). Fees vary widely and there's no official price list, so get a written quote (as of October 2026; check each provider). A consultant makes sense if you're also buying proposal-writing help. Paying only for registration rarely makes sense, because the wizard itself is free. One limitation: a consultant can't be your legal representative or, for a natural person, your LEAR, so you'll still sign and verify the documents yourself.

Related guides on this site

  • EU Funding for SMEs: 7 Open 2026 Calls and How to Qualify

FAQ

How do I register on the EU Funding and Tenders Portal?

Create an EU Login at webgate.ec.europa.eu/cas, set up two-factor authentication, then sign in to the Participant Register and click Register your organisation. The 6-step wizard ends with a PIC on screen. Validation and the LEAR appointment come later, if your proposal is selected.

How do I sign up for the EU Funding and Tenders Portal?

Signing up means creating a personal EU Login with your name, email and a verification code, then activating it through the email link. That lets you log in, but it doesn't register your organisation. For that you need a PIC from the Participant Register.

What is the EU Funding and Tenders Portal Participant Register?

It's the Portal tool where organisations register, get a PIC and update their legal data. It also handles all communication with the Central Validation Service, including document requests and LEAR appointments (Online Manual).

How do I register an organization on the EU Funding & Tenders Portal?

Search for an existing PIC first. If there isn't one, enter the exact legal name and VAT number, the registered address and language, the legal form, and the authorised users, then check the summary and submit. Use the legal name from your trade register extract, not your brand name, so validation goes through later.

item.title: EU Funding for SMEs: 7 Open 2026 Calls and How to Qualify
item.dc:creator: Aoba Works
item.description: EU funding for SMEs in late 2026: 7 open calls from EIC Accelerator to Digital Europe, matched to company size and country, with eligibility steps to check before you apply.
item.content:encoded:
How this guide was made: drafted with AI assistance from the official sources linked below, then passed an automated editorial check before publishing. Our process

EU funding for SMEs in late 2026 comes in three main forms. There are direct grants from Brussels-managed programmes (EIC Accelerator, Digital Europe, Horizon Europe, the Single Market Programme), small vouchers such as the EUIPO SME Fund, and EU-backed loans and equity that you get through your local bank or fund. As of 20 October 2026, at least seven calls are open or still reachable for SMEs, with deadlines running from 4 November 2026 to 2 February 2027. To qualify you must meet the official SME definition (fewer than 250 staff, plus ≤€50M turnover or ≤€43M balance sheet), be established in an eligible country, and register a PIC on the Funding & Tenders Portal.

Which option is right for you?

Choose by your stage and what you need the money for. Start with the call that matches your situation, and leave the rest for later.

Your situationWhat to pick firstFirst page to open
Beginner, micro or small firm, needs trade marks or patents protectedEUIPO SME Fund 2026 (Voucher 3 patents is still listed as open)EUIPO SME Fund 2026
Deep-tech startup at TRL 6+ that wants to scaleEIC Accelerator (short proposal now, full proposal at a later cut-off)EIC Accelerator
Cybersecurity or AI company building tools for other SMEsDigital Europe AI4SME call (DIGITAL-ECCC-2027-DEPLOY-CYBER-11-AI4SME)ECCC call announcement
Spin-off or SME holding results from an earlier Horizon/H2020 projectHorizon Europe "Proof of market" (HORIZON-CL4-2027-01-MAT-PROD-49)Knowledge valorisation in WP 2026-2027
University or tech-transfer office"Unlocking academic IP" (MAT-PROD-42) or Venture Builders (MAT-PROD-50)Same knowledge valorisation page
Tight budget, can't co-fund a grantFree advice from the Enterprise Europe Network first, then EU-backed loansaccess2finance
Grant consultant screening calls for clientsFunding & Tenders Portal search filtered to "Open for submission"Funding & Tenders Portal

If none of these match, a new founder can still look at Erasmus for Young Entrepreneurs, a Single Market Programme exchange that places you with a host entrepreneur abroad for 1 to 6 months (European Commission).

What Is EU Funding and How Does It Work for SMEs?

EU funding means grants, equity or guarantees paid from the EU budget. It reaches you either directly from the Commission and its agencies or through national and regional authorities. Which route applies decides where you apply and which rules you follow.

Direct (centralised) management. The Commission or an executive agency publishes calls, evaluates proposals and signs grant agreements. EISMEA, for example, runs the EIC and the Single Market Programme's SME strand. All of these calls sit on one site, the Funding & Tenders Portal. The calls in this guide all use this route, except the EUIPO SME Fund, which runs on its own EUIPO site.

Shared management. Cohesion funds such as the ERDF are spent by national or regional managing authorities, so their calls appear on national portals, not the EU portal. These schemes usually count as state aid. Small amounts often go out under the de minimis rule, which caps aid at €300,000 per undertaking over any three-year rolling period (EUR-Lex summary of Regulation 2023/2831).

Financial instruments. Loans, guarantees and equity under InvestEU never come from Brussels directly. They go through more than 1,000 partner banks, funds and investors that you find via access2finance (Enterprise Europe Brussels).

How a direct grant moves, in order:

  1. The Commission adopts a work programme listing topics and budgets.
  2. Each topic opens as a call on the portal with a fixed deadline (17:00 Brussels time in all the calls below).
  3. You submit through the portal, and independent experts score your proposal against published criteria.
  4. If you are selected, your organisation is validated, a LEAR is appointed, and you sign the grant agreement electronically.

For example, a company applying to the AI4SME cyber call submits by 14 January 2027, and evaluation is planned for February to April 2027 (ECCC call document via FFG). Plan your cash flow around a gap of several months between submission and money.

European Funding for SMEs: Which Programs Apply in 2026?

In late 2026 SMEs have four main programme routes: the EIC Accelerator, Digital Europe, Horizon Europe Cluster 4, and Single Market Programme-linked support. The EUIPO SME Fund covers IP costs on its own track. Each one fits a different stage of innovation.

The 7 calls open or reachable as of 20 October 2026

#Call (ID)Who it suitsMoneyDeadline
1EIC Accelerator Open / ChallengesSingle SMEs/startups, TRL 6–8Grant below €2.5M + equity €1–10MFull-proposal cut-off 4 Nov 2026; short proposals batched monthly
2DIGITAL-ECCC-2027-DEPLOY-CYBER-11-AI4SMECyber/AI firms building tools for SMEs€3–5M per project, 75% rate for SMEs14 Jan 2027
3DIGITAL-ECCC-2027-DEPLOY-CYBER-11-EULEGProjects on EU cybersecurity legislation compliance€20M topic budget14 Jan 2027
4HORIZON-CL4-2027-01-MAT-PROD-49 "Proof of market"Small consortia of spin-offs, startups, SMEsInnovation Action2 Feb 2027
5HORIZON-CL4-2027-01-MAT-PROD-47 Pilot access to Technology InfrastructuresInfrastructure operators serving startups/SMEsCoordination & Support Action2 Feb 2027
6HORIZON-CL4-2027-01-MAT-PROD-42 Unlocking academic IPUniversities, industry, SMEsSee topic page2 Feb 2027
7EUIPO SME Fund 2026Any EU or Ukrainian SMEPatents up to €3,500; plant varieties up to €1,5004 Dec 2026 or until funds run out

Sources: EIC figures from the EIC Accelerator page. Cyber calls from the ECCC announcement and EuroAccess. Horizon topics from the Commission's valorisation page. SME Fund from marchistorici.com and Interpatent. All figures as of October 2026; check the official pages.

What each programme is for

EIC Accelerator. The 2026 budget is €634M: €414M for Accelerator Open and €220M for Challenges (Alien Technology Transfer summary of WP 2026). The minimum equity component went up from €0.5M in 2025 to €1M in 2026 (same source). This route suits companies that want investors and can show a path to scale. It is not for service businesses or projects that are still lab research.

Digital Europe. The programme funds the deployment of digital technology, not research. The ECCC's September 2026 round is worth €96M across seven topics, and €20M of it goes to AI4SME (ECCC). Note that the 10th DIGITAL round, worth about €45.4M, closed on 1 October 2026 (ONE Spain). If you were planning around it, wait for the next round.

Single Market Programme (SMP COSME). The 2026 SME calls have already closed. Tourism SMEs (SMP-COSME-2026-TOURSME-01) closed on 20 May 2026 and Agri-food Biotech Scaling-up on 2 June 2026 (EuroAccess; EISMEA). For the rest of 2026, the SMP mostly reaches SMEs through the Enterprise Europe Network and Erasmus for Young Entrepreneurs, not through new grant calls.

Horizon Europe Cluster 4. These calls usually need a consortium and a Part B written to the scoring criteria. If you are new to that format, read our Horizon Europe Proposal Template Part B: 2026 Scoring Map before drafting.

EU Funding for Small Business: Eligibility by Size and Country

Small-business eligibility depends on two things: the official SME definition and whether your country takes part in the specific programme. Being "small" under your national rules does not count.

The SME thresholds

CategoryStaff headcountTurnoveror Balance sheet
Micro< 10≤ €2M≤ €2M
Small< 50≤ €10M≤ €10M
Medium< 250≤ €50M≤ €43M

Source: Commission SME definition, Recommendation 2003/361. The staff ceiling always applies. Then you need to pass only one of the two financial tests, either turnover or balance sheet (same source).

The Commission has also introduced a "small mid-cap" category for firms that have outgrown SME status (same source). The EIC Accelerator accepts small mid-caps with up to 499 employees, but for the investment component only (EIC).

Country rules differ by programme

Programme / callWho can apply
EIC AcceleratorEU member states and Horizon Europe associated countries. Applicants from other countries can be eligible if they relocate (EIC)
Horizon Europe Cluster 4EU plus associated countries. Canada, New Zealand and South Korea are associated to Pillar II only (alientt.com list; official list: EC country participation PDF)
Digital Europe AI4SMEEU member states, EEA countries (Norway, Iceland, Liechtenstein) and overseas countries and territories (EuroAccess)
EUIPO SME FundSMEs established in the EU and Ukraine (Interpatent)

One consequence trips people up. Cluster 4 is Pillar II, so a Canadian or Korean SME can join a Cluster 4 project. The EIC Accelerator sits in Pillar III, so the same company cannot apply to it from home. The UK, Switzerland, Norway and Ukraine are on the associated list for the whole of Horizon Europe (same sources).

Pitfalls and fixes

  • You count only your own figures. If another company holds a stake in yours, its headcount and finances may have to be added to your figures (Commission). Fix: map your shareholders before you start the SME self-assessment.
  • A venture-backed startup assumes it is automatically an SME. A large corporate shareholder can push you over the thresholds. Fix: read the linked and partner enterprise chapter of the SME User Guide, which is linked from the same Commission page.
  • You rely on an old associated-country list. Association agreements change. Fix: check the official PDF on the call date, not a blog post.

EU Grants for SMEs vs. Loans and Equity: Which Should You Apply For?

Apply for a grant if you have a risky innovation project and can wait months for a decision. Go for an EU-backed loan or guarantee through a local intermediary if you need working capital or investment money sooner.

Direct EU grant (e.g. AI4SME, Horizon)EIC blended financeInvestEU-backed loan/equity
Where to applyFunding & Tenders PortalFunding & Tenders Portal + EIC platformYour bank, fund or VC via access2finance
DilutionNoneEquity €1–10M means investors take a stakeEquity products dilute; loans don't
Co-fundingYes. AI4SME funds 50%, or 75% for SMEsGrant is a lump sum below €2.5MThe intermediary sets the terms
SpeedMonths (AI4SME evaluation Feb–Apr 2027)Short proposal decision in 4–6 weeks, then several stagesSimilar to a normal bank decision
Best forR&D, deployment, consortium projectsScaling deep techEquipment, working capital, expansion

Sources: ECCC call document, EuroAccess, EIC, Enterprise Europe Brussels on access2finance.

How to decide:

  • Choose a grant if the project would not happen without public money and you can pay the uncovered share. At 75% funding, a €4M AI4SME project still leaves you €1M to fund yourself (example calculation).
  • Choose InvestEU-backed finance if the investment is commercially sound but your bank wants more collateral. The EU guarantee is designed to cover exactly that gap (EURA AG).
  • Choose EIC blended finance only if you are comfortable with the EIC Fund becoming a shareholder.

Pitfalls. Don't treat a grant as fast money: with the cyber calls, submission and signature are months apart. Also, access2finance does not lend anything itself. It lists intermediaries, and you apply directly to the institution you pick (Enterprise Europe Brussels).

EU Support for SMEs Beyond Grants: Advisory and Network Services

The cheapest EU support for SMEs is free advice. The Enterprise Europe Network gives partner matchmaking, internationalisation advice and funding guidance at no cost. It is active in more than 60 countries, with around 3,000 experts in more than 600 member organisations (Wikipedia summary; Lithuanian Innovation Centre, an EEN member).

What EEN can do for you:

  • Tell you which calls fit your company and country, including national schemes outside the EU portal.
  • Find consortium partners for Horizon or Digital Europe topics through its partnering database.
  • Review an application idea before you spend weeks writing it.

What it won't do: write your proposal for you. Its advisers are spread thin, so you need to come to them with a specific question.

Other no-cost routes:

  • National Contact Points (NCPs) for Horizon Europe and Digital Europe. They explain topic scope and eligibility. Flanders' NCP, for example, publishes notices about new Digital Europe calls (NCP Flanders).
  • Partner search on each topic page of the Funding & Tenders Portal, under "Partner search announcements".
  • Erasmus for Young Entrepreneurs, for founders and for experienced host entrepreneurs, with EU support towards travel and living costs (European Commission).

How to get EEN help:

  1. Open the Enterprise Europe Network site and find the local contact point for your region.
  2. Send a short email: your sector, headcount, TRL, and the call ID you are considering.
  3. Ask two questions: "Are we eligible?" and "Who else in the network is preparing a proposal on this topic?"

For example, a 30-person Polish cybersecurity firm could ask its local EEN office whether to apply to AI4SME alone or join a consortium. The call allows single applicants but says collaboration can strengthen implementation (EuroAccess).

EU Funding Requirements: Documents and Eligibility Checklist

Every direct EU call requires the same basics: an EU Login account, a 9-digit PIC, an SME self-assessment where SME status matters, and a proposal written to the topic text. Validation documents and a LEAR come later, only if you are selected.

Setup steps on the Funding & Tenders Portal

  1. Create an EU Login. On the portal, click "Login", then "Create an account". Use a work email that more than one person can reach if staff change.
  2. Search for an existing PIC. Under "How to participate" → "Participant Register", search your organisation's legal name first. Duplicate PICs cause delays (Funding & Tenders Online Manual).
  3. Register your organisation. The registration wizard asks for legal name, address, registration country and legal form. You get a 9-digit PIC straight away, but it stays provisional until validated (same source).
  4. Run the SME wizard. If you have no SME self-assessment from the last 2 years, the submission system prompts you to complete one. You enter headcount and financial figures for your last approved accounting period and for any linked enterprises (SME wizard guide; H2020 Online Manual).
  5. Prepare validation documents in advance. If you are selected, the Central Validation Service asks for proof of legal existence and, depending on the entity, financial or legal-status documents (Online Manual).
  6. Appoint a LEAR. Without a LEAR, you cannot update your legal entity data or sign contracts electronically (LEAR appointment).

Call-specific documents

  • Digital Europe AI4SME: Part B of at most 70 pages, plus a mandatory ownership control declaration (EuroAccess).
  • EIC Accelerator short proposal: a 12-page form, a 10-slide pitch deck and a 3-minute video (EIC).
  • EUIPO SME Fund: apply before you pay any IP fees, because paying first loses your right to reimbursement (marchistorici.com).

Common mistakes and fixes

MistakeFix
Registering on the deadline dayGet the PIC at least a week before. It is issued instantly, but EU Login and wizard problems take time
Your SME self-assessment is older than 2 yearsRedo it in the wizard. The system prompts you, but at a bad moment
Paying a trade mark or patent fee before applying for the voucherApply first, pay after approval
Submitting at 16:55 Brussels timeSubmit a draft early. You can resubmit until the deadline, and the latest version counts

How to Check If Your SME Qualifies for a Specific 2026 Call

Open the topic page on the Funding & Tenders Portal, read the "Conditions and documents" section, and check it against your country, legal form, TRL and consortium setup before you write a word. This takes about an hour and can save you weeks of drafting.

Step-by-step check

  1. Go to the Funding & Tenders Portal → "Search Funding & Tenders" → "Calls for proposals".
  2. Under "Submission status", tick "Open for submission". Add "Forthcoming" if you want to plan ahead.
  3. Under "Programme", choose for example "Digital Europe Programme (DIGITAL)" or "Horizon Europe (HORIZON)". Or paste a topic ID such as DIGITAL-ECCC-2027-DEPLOY-CYBER-11-AI4SME into the search box.
  4. On the topic page, read "Topic description" for the expected outcomes and scope. If your project doesn't produce those outcomes, stop here.
  5. Open "Conditions and documents". Check:
  6. Admissibility: page limits (70 for AI4SME).
  7. Eligible countries: EU/EEA for AI4SME; EU plus associated countries for Horizon.
  8. Other eligibility: single applicant allowed or minimum consortium, and any ownership control rules.
  9. Financial and operational capacity: SMEs often have to show their accounts.
  10. Check the "Type of action". An Innovation Action (IA) such as "Proof of market" means near-market work. A Coordination & Support Action (CSA) such as MAT-PROD-47 funds networking and services, not your own product development.
  11. Check TRL fit. The EIC Accelerator expects TRL 6–8 for its innovation activities (EIC).
  12. Check timing against the deadline. Then run steps 1–4 of the requirements checklist above.

Example: three applicants, one afternoon

These are illustrations only.

  • A Norwegian cyber SME with 40 staff. It can apply to AI4SME alone, because the EEA is eligible and single applicants are allowed. Its maximum rate is 75%.
  • A Canadian AI startup. It cannot apply to the EIC Accelerator from Canada because of Pillar III. It could join a Cluster 4 "Proof of market" consortium, because Canada is associated to Pillar II, as long as the topic's own conditions allow it.
  • A Spanish university. "Unlocking academic IP" (MAT-PROD-42) or "Venture Builders Network" (MAT-PROD-50) are a better fit than SME-only instruments. Both close on 2 February 2027 (Commission).

A note on EIC timing

The 4 November 2026 cut-off is for full proposals, and you can only send one after your short proposal is approved. Short-proposal decisions take 4–6 weeks (EIC). If you start today, you will realistically be aiming for a 2027 cut-off. Those dates depend on the next work programme, so confirm them once it is published.

Next steps

Pick one call from the table above and confirm your eligibility for it this week. Leave the drafting until that check is done.

Do it yourself today:

  1. Create your EU Login and search the Participant Register for an existing PIC. Register if there is none.
  2. Run the SME self-assessment wizard with your last approved accounts and any linked-company data.
  3. Open the topic page of your chosen call, read "Conditions and documents", and write down any requirement you don't meet yet.

If you would rather not do it yourself:

  • Enterprise Europe Network and National Contact Points. Free. Good for eligibility checks and partner searches. Not for anyone who wants a proposal written for them, because they don't draft proposals.
  • Private grant consultancies. Most charge a fixed fee, a success fee, or both. There is no official price list, so ask for a written quote (as of October 2026; check each firm's terms). They suit teams with a strong project and no writing capacity. They don't suit very early ideas, because a consultant can't fix weak eligibility or a poor fit with the topic. No consultant can guarantee selection.
  • EIC Business Acceleration Services. Coaching and investor events for companies that already hold EIC funding. Not available before you are selected (EIC).

Related guides on this site:

  • Horizon Europe Proposal Template Part B: 2026 Scoring Map, for anyone drafting a Cluster 4 "Proof of market" or academic IP proposal.

FAQ

What is the EU definition of an SME for funding purposes?

An SME has fewer than 250 staff and either turnover of €50M or less or a balance sheet of €43M or less, under Recommendation 2003/361. Micro firms are under 10 staff and small firms under 50, with lower financial ceilings. Figures from linked or partner enterprises may have to be added to yours (Commission).

Can non-EU companies apply for EU SME funding?

Yes, if their country is associated to the right programme or part of it. Horizon Europe associated countries such as the UK, Switzerland, Norway and Ukraine can access the EIC. Canada and South Korea are associated to Pillar II only. AI4SME is open to the EU and EEA, and the EUIPO SME Fund to the EU and Ukraine.

How much funding can an SME get from the EIC Accelerator?

A grant component below €2.5M as a lump sum, plus optional equity of €1M to €10M. Larger rounds are possible through STEP ScaleUp (EIC). The 2026 Accelerator budget is €634M in total.

Do I need a partner organization to apply for EU SME grants?

Not always. The EIC Accelerator is for single companies, and AI4SME allows single applicants. Many Horizon Europe Innovation Actions need a consortium, so read "Conditions and documents" on the topic page before you look for partners.

Is EU funding for SMEs taxable or does it affect state aid limits?

How a grant is taxed depends on your national law, so ask your accountant how it will be booked. Funding from national or regional schemes, including cohesion funds, often falls under de minimis, which caps aid at €300,000 per undertaking over three rolling years (EUR-Lex). If your project mixes national co-funding with an EU grant, check the state-aid position with your managing authority or national contact point (Irish DETE guidance).
